docs.title: PKI Framework
docs.text:
PKI Framework reads, writes and validates the structures a public key infrastructure is made of: X.509 certificates, attribute certificates, certification requests, the ASN.1 types underneath them, and the textual encodings they travel in. It is a library of data structures and a validator, in pure PHP.

composer require spomky-labs/pki-framework

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Certificate;

$certificate = Certificate::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('server.crt'));

echo $certificate->tbsCertificate()->subject()->toString();   // cn=example.com
echo $certificate->tbsCertificate()->validity()->notAfter()->dateTime()->format('c');

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text: Specification What the library does with it X.690 ASN.1 DER encoding and decoding, every universal type, tagged types, indefinite length RFC 5280 X.509 certificates, their extensions, and certification path validation RFC 5755 Attribute certificates and their validation RFC 2986 PKCS #10 certification requests RFC 5208, RFC 5958 PKCS #8 private keys, one asymmetric key RFC 7468 PEM, the textual encoding of all of the above X.501, X.520 Distinguished names, attribute types, name comparison and string preparation RFC 8410 Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 keys

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Reading material you were handed — Reading a certificate, then Textual encoding (PEM).
  • Checking that a chain leads somewhere you trust — Validating a path. Read What validation does not do before you rely on it.
  • Issuing certificates — Issuing a certificate, and Issuing from a request when the subject sent a CSR.
  • Working one level down, on the ASN.1 itself — ASN.1 and DER.

docs.title: Two things to know before you build on it
docs.text:
The library never opens a network connection. Nothing is fetched from an authority information access extension, a CRL distribution point or an OCSP responder, and no system trust store is read. Everything the library trusts, the trust anchors included, is handed to it by your application. Path validation therefore says nothing about revocation; see What validation does not do.

Everything a certification request contains was chosen by whoever submitted it. TBSCertificate::fromCSR() does not verify its signature and never copies the extensions that decide what a certificate may do. Name the ones you are willing to honour; see Issuing from a request.

docs.title: Credit
docs.text: The framework started as a fork of the libraries published at github.com/sop by Joni Eskelinen. It has diverged substantially since — the code has been reworked, extended and maintained to meet the Spomky-Labs requirements — and the two are no longer interchangeable. All credit for the original work goes to its developer. Migrating from the sop libraries describes what changed.

docs.title: ASN.1 and DER
docs.text:
Everything in a public key infrastructure is an ASN.1 structure encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules of X.690. SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1 is that layer, and the rest of the library is built on it.

You rarely need it to read a certificate — Certificate does that for you. You need it when you meet a structure the library does not model: a private extension, an OtherName, an attribute whose syntax is yours.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
Every type is an Element. An element knows its tag and can encode itself:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Constructed\Sequence;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\Integer;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\ObjectIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\UTF8String;

$sequence = Sequence::create(
    ObjectIdentifier::create('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1'),
    Integer::create(42),
    UTF8String::create('hello')
);

$der = $sequence->toDER();
$again = Element::fromDER($der);

$again->tag() === Element::TYPE_SEQUENCE;   // true

There is no constructor to call: every type is built with create(), and decoded with fromDER().

docs.title: UnspecifiedType
docs.text:
Decoding gives back something whose type is not known until you look at it. Rather than hand you an Element to test by hand, the library hands you an UnspecifiedType: a wrapper whose as*() methods each assert one type and return it.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\UnspecifiedType;

$element = UnspecifiedType::fromDER($der);

$sequence = $element->asSequence();              // UnexpectedValueException if it is not one
$oid = $sequence->at(0)->asObjectIdentifier();   // at() returns an UnspecifiedType too
$count = $sequence->at(1)->asInteger()->intNumber();
$text = $sequence->at(2)->asUTF8String()->string();

Structure::at() returns an UnspecifiedType, so reading into a structure reads as a chain of assertions. Each one throws UnexpectedValueException when the material is not shaped the way the page of the specification says it is — which is what you want when the material came from outside.

$element->asUnspecified() goes the other way, from an Element you already hold.

docs.title: Structures
docs.text:
Sequence and Set extend Structure, which is Countable and IteratorAggregate, and immutable like everything else:

$sequence = Sequence::create(Integer::create(1));

$sequence = $sequence->withAppended(Integer::create(2));
$sequence = $sequence->withReplaced(0, Integer::create(0));
$sequence = $sequence->withoutElement(1);

count($sequence);                 // 1
$sequence->has(0, Element::TYPE_INTEGER);  // true: present, and of that type

Structure::explodeDER() splits the DER of a structure into the DER of each of its children, without decoding them.

docs.text:

  • Encoding and decoding — DER in and out, offsets, DERData, indefinite length.
  • Tagging — implicit and explicit tags, context-specific, application and private classes.
  • Decoding untrusted input — the limits to set before you decode what a stranger sent.

docs.title: Encoding and decoding
docs.text: The library speaks the Distinguished Encoding Rules. DER is BER with every choice removed — one encoding per value — which is what makes a signature over a structure meaningful.

docs.title: Out
docs.text:
toDER() on any element:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Constructed\Sequence;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\Integer;

$der = Sequence::create(Integer::create(1), Integer::create(2))->toDER();

Every structure of the X.509 layer has a toASN1() that gives you its Sequence, so toDER() follows from it:

$der = $certificate->toASN1()->toDER();   // the same bytes as $certificate->toDER()

docs.title: In
docs.text:
Element::fromDER() decodes one element:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;

$element = Element::fromDER($der);

Called on a concrete class, it also asserts the type:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Constructed\Sequence;

$sequence = Sequence::fromDER($der);   // UnexpectedValueException if the data is not a SEQUENCE

Anything malformed raises DecodeException, and nothing else escapes fromDER(): the type-specific decoders reach into large-number arithmetic, into constructors and into string validation, any of which may signal malformed input in its own way, and the exception is normalised on the way out with the original kept as its previous.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Exception\DecodeException;

try {
    $element = Element::fromDER($bytes);
} catch (DecodeException $e) {
    // not DER, or not DER shaped the way this type is
}

docs.title: Several elements in one string
docs.text:
fromDER() takes an offset by reference and moves it past what it read, so a concatenation is read in a loop:

$offset = 0;
$elements = [];

while ($offset < strlen($der)) {
    $elements[] = Element::fromDER($der, $offset);
}

To split a structure without decoding its children, Structure::explodeDER() returns the DER of each one:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Structure;

foreach (Structure::explodeDER($der) as $childDer) {
    // one encoded child at a time
}

docs.title: Carrying an encoding you do not want to decode
docs.text:
DERData is an element whose content is DER you already hold. It encodes to exactly those bytes and decodes nothing:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\DERData;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Constructed\Sequence;

$sequence = Sequence::create(DERData::create($opaqueDer));

Use it to put a structure the library does not model inside one it does — the value of a private extension, for instance — without a round trip through types you would have to write.

docs.title: Indefinite length
docs.text:
BER allows a constructed element to declare no length and end with an end-of-contents marker. DER does not. The library reads both and lets you ask and set:

$element->hasIndefiniteLength();              // what was read
$element = $element->withIndefiniteLength();  // encode it that way

Leave it alone for anything you sign or send: a structure whose length is indefinite is not DER, and a verifier that re-encodes it will not get your bytes back.

docs.title: Tag checks
docs.text:
$element->tag();                            // the tag number
$element->isType(Element::TYPE_SEQUENCE);   // a question
$element->expectType(Element::TYPE_SEQUENCE); // an assertion, throws otherwise
$element->isTagged();                       // not a universal type
Element::tagToName(Element::TYPE_SEQUENCE); // "SEQUENCE", for an error message

expectType() accepts the pseudotypes as well as the real ones.

docs.title: Tagging
docs.text: A SEQUENCE whose fields are optional needs a way to tell them apart, and ASN.1 does it with tags. Half the fields of an X.509 structure are tagged, so reading one by hand means knowing which kind of tag it carries.

docs.title: Explicit and implicit
docs.text:
An explicit tag wraps the value: the tag is added around an encoding that still says what the value is. An implicit tag replaces the value's own tag: nothing in the bytes says what is inside, so the reader has to know from the specification.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\Integer;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Tagged\ExplicitlyTaggedType;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Tagged\ImplicitlyTaggedType;

$explicit = ExplicitlyTaggedType::create(0, Integer::create(42));
$implicit = ImplicitlyTaggedType::create(1, Integer::create(42));

Reading one back, you say which it is and — for an implicit tag — what is inside:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;

$tagged = $element->expectTagged(0);          // a tagged type, tag 0
$value = $tagged->asExplicit()->asInteger();  // unwrap, then assert the type

$tagged = $element->expectTagged(1);
$value = $tagged->asImplicit(Element::TYPE_INTEGER)->asInteger();

asExplicit() and asImplicit() return an UnspecifiedType, so the as*() chain continues. The expect* variants — expectExplicit(), expectImplicit() — return the tagging interface itself when you want to work with it rather than with the value.

An implicit tag read as explicit decodes garbage, not an error

The bytes inside an implicitly tagged element are the content of the value, with no identifier of their own. Reading them as if they were a complete element may well succeed and give you something unrelated. The specification says which kind of tag a field carries; follow it.

docs.title: The tag classes
docs.text:
Class Constant Where you meet it Universal Identifier::CLASS_UNIVERSAL the built-in types: INTEGER, SEQUENCE, … Context-specific Identifier::CLASS_CONTEXT_SPECIFIC the optional fields of almost every X.509 structure Application Identifier::CLASS_APPLICATION rare; some older PKCS structures Private Identifier::CLASS_PRIVATE never, unless your own schema uses it

Context-specific is the default of ExplicitlyTaggedType::create() and ImplicitlyTaggedType::create(), which is why the examples above pass only a number. The other classes have their own wrappers, ApplicationType and PrivateType, reached with asApplication() and asPrivate().

$element->typeClass() === Identifier::CLASS_CONTEXT_SPECIFIC;

docs.title: Reading an optional field
docs.text:
Structure::hasTagged() and getTagged() find a field by its tag:

if ($sequence->hasTagged(3)) {
    $extensions = $sequence->getTagged(3)->asExplicit()->asSequence();
}

A repeated tag is not a field

The optional fields of a structure are distinct, so the same tag twice is not a field but a second copy of one. hasTagged() keeps only the last and would silently drop what came before, which is why the X.509 decoders of this library call assertUniqueTaggedElements() first. Do the same when you decode a structure whose fields must each appear once:

$sequence->assertUniqueTaggedElements('TBSCertificate');

The string names the structure in the exception message.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
TBSCertificate holds its extensions in field [3], explicitly tagged. Reading them without the X.509 layer:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Constructed\Sequence;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extensions;

$certificate = Sequence::fromDER($der);           // Certificate
$tbs = $certificate->at(0)->asSequence();         // TBSCertificate
$tbs->assertUniqueTaggedElements('TBSCertificate');

$extensions = $tbs->hasTagged(3)
    ? Extensions::fromASN1($tbs->getTagged(3)->asExplicit()->asSequence())
    : Extensions::create();

In practice, Certificate::fromDER($der)->tbsCertificate()->extensions() is that, already done and checked. Go down to this level for a structure the library does not model.

docs.title: The types
docs.text: Every universal type of X.690 has a class under SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type. Each is built with create(), each knows its tag, and each is immutable.

docs.title: Primitive types
docs.text:
ASN.1 type Class Built from Read with BOOLEAN Primitive\Boolean bool value(): bool INTEGER Primitive\Integer int, numeric string, BigInteger number(): string, intNumber(): int, getValue(): BigInteger ENUMERATED Primitive\Enumerated as Integer as Integer BIT STRING Primitive\BitString string and a count of unused bits string(), numBits(), testBit(), range() OCTET STRING Primitive\OctetString string string() NULL Primitive\NullType nothing — OBJECT IDENTIFIER Primitive\ObjectIdentifier dotted string oid(): string RELATIVE-OID Primitive\RelativeOID dotted string oid(): string ObjectDescriptor Primitive\ObjectDescriptor string descriptor(): string REAL Primitive\Real fromFloat(), fromString() floatVal(), mantissa(), exponent(), base() EOC Primitive\EOC nothing —

An INTEGER never comes back as a PHP integer unless you ask for one. A serial number or an RSA modulus does not fit, so number() returns a decimal string and getValue() a brick/math BigInteger. intNumber() throws when the value does not fit in a PHP integer.

docs.title: String types
docs.text:
Each carries the character set its tag promises, and refuses a string outside it.

ASN.1 type Class UTF8String Primitive\UTF8String PrintableString Primitive\PrintableString NumericString Primitive\NumericString IA5String Primitive\IA5String VisibleString Primitive\VisibleString GeneralString Primitive\GeneralString GraphicString Primitive\GraphicString BMPString Primitive\BMPString UniversalString Primitive\UniversalString T61String Primitive\T61String VideotexString Primitive\VideotexString CharacterString Primitive\CharacterString

They all extend BaseString, so string() gives the value and (string) works. The StringType interface marks them, and the time types with them, for a signature that takes any of them.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\PrintableString;

$string = PrintableString::create('FR');
echo $string->string();    // FR
echo $string;              // FR

A PrintableString built from a value its character set forbids throws rather than encode something a peer would read differently.

docs.title: Time types
Constructed types
Pseudotypes
docs.text:
Three tags are not ASN.1 types but expectations you can pass to expectType():

Constant Matches Element::TYPE_STRING any string type Element::TYPE_TIME UTCTime or GeneralizedTime Element::TYPE_CONSTRUCTED_STRING a string in constructed form 
$element->expectType(Element::TYPE_STRING);

docs.title: Bit flags
docs.text:
A BIT STRING that carries named flags — keyUsage, for one — is easier to read through Flags:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Util\Flags;

$flags = Flags::fromBitString($bitString, 9);
$flags->test(0);           // the first bit, as the specification numbers them
echo $flags->string();     // the bits as a byte string

The extensions that carry flags already do this for you: see KeyUsageExtension.

docs.title: Decoding untrusted input
docs.text:
A certificate chain arrives from a peer. A certification request arrives from a form. A DER string is a recursive, self-describing format, and decoding one is work an attacker gets to choose the shape of.

This page is what to set before you decode material you did not produce. The security recommendations list the rest.

docs.title: What the library bounds for you
docs.text:
Nesting depth. Decoding a constructed type recurses, so an attacker who sends a thousand nested SEQUENCE headers in a few kilobytes would exhaust the stack. The decoder counts levels and refuses beyond Element::DEFAULT_MAX_NESTING_DEPTH, which is 64. Every decoded element takes a level, the end-of-contents marker of an indefinite length encoding included.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;

Element::maxNestingDepth();      // 64
Element::setMaxNestingDepth(16); // a real X.509 structure rarely nests deeper than ten

The cap is global process state

setMaxNestingDepth() is static and affects every later decode in the process, including the ones inside the X.509 layer. Set it once at boot. Set it too low and legitimate material stops decoding.

Exception type. Nothing but DecodeException escapes Element::fromDER(). The type-specific decoders reach into large-number arithmetic, into constructors and into string validation, any of which may signal malformed input in its own way; the exception is normalised on the way out, with the original kept as its previous. So one catch is enough:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Exception\DecodeException;

try {
    $certificate = Certificate::fromDER($bytes);
} catch (DecodeException $e) {
    // malformed; $e->getPrevious() says what the decoder tripped on
}

Repeated optional fields. The X.509 decoders call assertUniqueTaggedElements() before they read optional fields, so a structure carrying the same tag twice is refused rather than read as its last copy. See Tagging.

Encodings that are not DER. A type X.690 only ever allows in primitive form is refused in constructed form, a SET OF must be sorted, and a string type refuses a value outside its character set.

docs.title: What you have to bound
docs.text:
Size. The library decodes the string you hand it; it does not know where the string came from. A hundred megabytes of valid, deeply fanned-out DER is a hundred megabytes of PHP objects. Cap the length before you decode:

if (strlen($bytes) > 64 * 1024) {
    throw new RuntimeException('Certificate material too large.');
}

A certificate is a few kilobytes. A chain is a few more. Pick a limit from what your protocol actually carries, not from what might fit.

Count. A PEM bundle holds as many blocks as the file has. Reading one from a peer means reading whatever number they chose:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEMBundle;

$bundle = PEMBundle::fromString($chainFromPeer);

if (count($bundle) > 10) {
    throw new RuntimeException('Too many certificates in the chain.');
}

Time. Path validation walks a policy tree whose size depends on the certificates in the path. PathValidationConfig::withMaxLength() bounds the path — the default is 3 — and bounding the input bounds the rest. See Configuration.

docs.title: What decoding does not tell you
docs.text:
Decoding says the bytes are well-formed. It says nothing about whether the structure means anything:

  • a certificate that decodes may be expired, revoked, self-signed by a stranger, or signed with an algorithm you do not accept;
  • a certification request that decodes may carry a signature that does not verify — verify() is a separate call;
  • a chain that decodes may lead nowhere you trust.

Decode, then validate. The two are different steps and the library keeps them apart on purpose.

docs.title: Attribute certificates
docs.text:
A public key certificate says this key belongs to this subject. An attribute certificate says this subject has these attributes — a role, a group, a clearance — and it carries no key of its own.

It is an authorisation statement bound to an identity someone else already certified. RFC 5755 defines them.

AttributeCertificate
├── AttributeCertificateInfo    holder, issuer, validity, the attributes, extensions
├── AlgorithmIdentifier
└── Signature

Same split as everywhere: AttributeCertificateInfo builds, AttributeCertificate is signed.

docs.title: Reading one
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\AttributeCertificate;

$ac = AttributeCertificate::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('role.ac'));   // label: ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE

$acinfo = $ac->acinfo();
$acinfo->holder();
$acinfo->issuer();
$acinfo->serialNumber();
$acinfo->validityPeriod()->notBeforeTime();
$acinfo->attributes();
$acinfo->extensions();

docs.title: The holder
docs.text:
The holder is not a name but a reference to a public key certificate, by any of three routes:

$holder = $acinfo->holder();

$holder->hasBaseCertificateID();   // the (issuer, serial) of the holder's certificate
$holder->baseCertificateID();
$holder->hasEntityName();          // a GeneralNames
$holder->entityName();
$holder->hasObjectDigestInfo();    // a digest of the object held
$holder->objectDigestInfo();

And the question you actually want:

$ac->isHeldBy($holderCertificate);   // does this AC belong to that certificate?
$ac->isIssuedBy($issuerCertificate);

docs.title: The issuer
docs.text:
An attribute authority, identified by its own public key certificate:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\AttCertIssuer;

AttCertIssuer::fromPKC($authorityCertificate);   // what you want
AttCertIssuer::fromName($name);                  // the v1 form, by name alone

An attribute authority is not a CA

Validation refuses an issuer certificate whose basicConstraints says cA:TRUE. An attribute authority signs attribute certificates; it does not issue public key certificates. Its keyUsage, if it has one, must permit digitalSignature or nonRepudiation — RFC 5755 section 4.5 accepts either.

docs.title: The attributes
docs.text:
Attributes here is a SequenceOfAttributes with shortcuts for the attributes RFC 5755 defines:

$attributes = $acinfo->attributes();

$attributes->hasRole();
$attributes->role();                       // a RoleAttributeValue
$attributes->roles();                      // all of them
$attributes->hasGroup();
$attributes->group();
$attributes->hasAccessIdentity();
$attributes->hasChargingIdentity();
$attributes->hasAuthenticationInformation();
Class, under AttributeCertificate\Attribute Carries RoleAttributeValue a role name, and optionally the authority that defines it GroupAttributeValue group membership AccessIdentityAttributeValue an identity for access control ChargingIdentityAttributeValue an identity for billing AuthenticationInfoAttributeValue authentication information

The last three share the SvceAuthInfo syntax — a service, an identity and optional auth info. The first two use the IETF attribute syntax, IetfAttrSyntax, whose values are IetfAttrValue: an octet string, an OID or a UTF-8 string, which isOctets(), isOID() and isString() tell apart.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Attribute\RoleAttributeValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\UniformResourceIdentifier;

$role = RoleAttributeValue::create(UniformResourceIdentifier::create('urn:roles:administrator'));
$role->roleName();
$role->hasRoleAuthority();

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
The same Extensions as a certificate, with two that matter here:

  • TargetInformationExtension — the servers or services this AC is meant for. Validation checks it against the targets you configured;
  • NoRevocationAvailableExtension — this AC is not revocable.

A critical extension the validator does not process makes validation fail, as RFC 5755 section 5 check 7 requires: an attribute certificate carries authorisation, and a critical extension is how its issuer narrows that authorisation. Accepting one that cannot be processed would grant the attributes unconditionally. The validator processes exactly those two; declare any others with ACValidationConfig::withAdditionalCriticalExtensions().

docs.title: Verifying and validating
docs.text:
$ac->verify($authorityPublicKeyInfo);   // the signature alone

As with certificates, that is one fact and not an authorisation decision. Validating an attribute certificate means validating two certification paths — the holder's and the issuer's — and more. See Validating an attribute certificate.

docs.title: In and out
docs.text:
AttributeCertificate::fromPEM($pem);
AttributeCertificate::fromDER($der);
AttributeCertificate::fromASN1($sequence);

$ac->toPEM()->string();
$ac->toDER();
echo $ac;

docs.title: Issuing an attribute certificate
docs.text: You are an attribute authority: a holder already has a public key certificate, and you want to say something about them.

docs.title: The whole thing
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature\SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\AttCertIssuer;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\AttCertValidityPeriod;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Attribute\RoleAttributeValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\AttributeCertificateInfo;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Attributes;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Holder;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\IssuerSerial;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\UniformResourceIdentifier;

$acinfo = AttributeCertificateInfo::create(
    Holder::create(IssuerSerial::fromPKC($holderCertificate)),
    AttCertIssuer::fromPKC($authorityCertificate),
    AttCertValidityPeriod::fromStrings('now', 'now + 8 hours'),
    Attributes::fromAttributeValues(
        RoleAttributeValue::create(UniformResourceIdentifier::create('urn:roles:administrator'))
    )
);

$ac = $acinfo->sign(
    SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(),
    $authorityPrivateKeyInfo
);

file_put_contents('role.ac', $ac->toPEM()->string());

Four arguments to create(): holder, issuer, validity, attributes.

docs.title: The holder
docs.text:
IssuerSerial::fromPKC() is the one to use: it ties the attribute certificate to one specific public key certificate, by its issuer and serial number.

Holder::create(IssuerSerial::fromPKC($holderCertificate));

The alternatives exist because the ASN.1 offers them, and are looser:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DirectoryName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralNames;

Holder::create(null, GeneralNames::create(DirectoryName::create($name)));   // by name

Naming a holder by name binds to whoever holds that name

A baseCertificateID names one certificate. An entityName names a subject, and any certificate with that subject — from any CA your relying parties trust — satisfies it. Prefer IssuerSerial::fromPKC().

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
AttCertValidityPeriod::fromStrings('now', 'now + 8 hours');
AttCertValidityPeriod::create($notBefore, $notAfter);   // two DateTimeImmutable

Unlike a certificate's Validity, both fields are GeneralizedTime, so there is no 2050 question.

Keep it short. An attribute certificate carries authorisation, there is nothing to revoke it with, and a validity period is the only expiry it has.

docs.title: The attributes
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Attribute\GroupAttributeValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Attribute\IetfAttrValue;

Attributes::fromAttributeValues(
    RoleAttributeValue::create(UniformResourceIdentifier::create('urn:roles:administrator')),
    GroupAttributeValue::create(IetfAttrValue::fromString('engineering'))
);

RoleAttributeValue::create() takes an optional second argument, the GeneralNames of the authority that defines the role — useful when the role namespace is not yours.

docs.title: The serial number
docs.text:
$acinfo = $acinfo->withRandomSerialNumber();      // 20 octets
$acinfo = $acinfo->withSerialNumber('12345');

As with certificates, sign() draws a 20-octet random serial number when none is set, and a size below MIN_RANDOM_SERIAL_SIZE — nine octets — raises a deprecation notice. See Issuing a certificate.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
targetInformation says which servers or services the attribute certificate is meant for. Validation checks it against the targets the verifier configured, so an AC captured from one service is not usable at another:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Target\TargetName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Target\Targets;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\TargetInformationExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;

$acinfo = $acinfo->withAdditionalExtensions(
    TargetInformationExtension::create(true, Targets::create(
        TargetName::create(DNSName::create('app.example.com'))
    ))
);

Mark it critical: a verifier that cannot process it must then refuse the AC rather than honour it everywhere.

docs.title: Not revocable
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\NoRevocationAvailableExtension;

$acinfo = $acinfo->withAdditionalExtensions(NoRevocationAvailableExtension::create(false));

An honest statement rather than a restriction: it tells a verifier not to look for a revocation list that does not exist.

docs.title: Extensions in general
docs.text:
$acinfo = $acinfo->withExtensions($extensions);          // replaces the set
$acinfo = $acinfo->withAdditionalExtensions(...$exts);   // adds to it

Do not sign a critical extension a verifier cannot process

The validator refuses an attribute certificate carrying a critical extension it does not handle, and it handles exactly targetInformation and noRevAvail. A critical extension of your own makes the AC unusable unless every verifier declares it with ACValidationConfig::withAdditionalCriticalExtensions() and implements the check.

docs.title: The signing certificate
docs.text:
Your attribute authority certificate has to pass the issuer profile of RFC 5755 section 4.5, or no conforming verifier will accept what you sign:

  • not a CA — basicConstraints with cA:TRUE is refused;
  • keyUsage, if present, permits digitalSignature or nonRepudiation.
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\BasicConstraintsExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\KeyUsageExtension;

// when issuing the attribute authority's own certificate
BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false);
KeyUsageExtension::create(true, KeyUsageExtension::DIGITAL_SIGNATURE);

docs.title: Checking what you made
docs.text:
$ac->verify($authorityPrivateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo());   // true
$ac->isHeldBy($holderCertificate);                        // true
$ac->isIssuedBy($authorityCertificate);                   // true

Then validate it the way a verifier would: Validating an attribute certificate.

docs.title: Validating an attribute certificate
docs.text: Validating an attribute certificate means validating two certification paths — the holder's and the issuer's — and then six more checks on top.

docs.title: The call
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Validation\ACValidationConfig;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Validation\ACValidator;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\AttributeCertificate\Validation\Exception\ACValidationException;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\CertificationPath;

$holderPath = CertificationPath::toTarget($holderCertificate, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);
$issuerPath = CertificationPath::toTarget($authorityCertificate, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);

$config = ACValidationConfig::create($holderPath, $issuerPath)
    ->withTrustedAttributeAuthorities($authorityCertificate)   // see below — do not skip this
    ->withTargets(TargetName::create(DNSName::create('app.example.com')));

try {
    $validated = ACValidator::create($ac, $config)->validate();
} catch (ACValidationException $e) {
    // not authorised
}

validate() returns the attribute certificate, or throws. Pass a crypto engine as the third argument of create() to use your own.

docs.title: The check you have to configure
docs.text:
Without withTrustedAttributeAuthorities(), any end-entity certificate will do

RFC 5755 section 5 check 4 says the attribute certificate's issuer must be directly trusted as an attribute authority. The validator cannot know who you trust, so without this call it skips the check — and then accepts whatever end-entity certificate the issuer path happens to end in.

Any certificate from any CA in your trust store would then be able to grant any role.

$config = $config->withTrustedAttributeAuthorities($authorityA, $authorityB);
$config->trustedAttributeAuthorities();   // a CertificateBundle, or null

The check is CertificateBundle::contains(), so it is an exact match on the encoding.

docs.title: What the validator checks
docs.text:
In order:

  1. The holder's certification path validates, and $ac->isHeldBy() that path's end-entity certificate. A path failure is wrapped: Failed to validate holder PKC's certification path.
  2. The issuer's certification path validates, and $ac->isIssuedBy() its end-entity certificate.
  3. The issuer profile, RFC 5755 section 4.5: the issuer certificate is not a CA, and its keyUsage, if present, permits digitalSignature or nonRepudiation.
  4. The attribute authority is trusted, if you configured the bundle.
  5. The AC's own signature, under the same policy as the paths — see below.
  6. The validity period contains the evaluation time.
  7. The targets match, if the AC carries a targetInformation extension.
  8. Every critical extension is one the validator processes, or one you declared.

The AC's own signature is held to the path policy

The attribute authority's key is never a working key of either path, so its size would never have been measured, and the crypto engine would happily verify an MD5 signature. The signature that carries the authorisation is checked against the same allowedSignatureAlgorithms() and minimumRSAKeySize() as the paths — which is a reason to hand the config a hardened PathValidationConfig.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
$config = ACValidationConfig::create($holderPath, $issuerPath);

$config = $config->withPathValidationConfig($pathConfig);
$config = $config->withEvaluationTime(new DateTimeImmutable('2026-06-01'));
$config = $config->withTrustedAttributeAuthorities(...$certificates);
$config = $config->withTargets(...$targets);
$config = $config->withAdditionalCriticalExtensions('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.7');

$config->holderPath();
$config->issuerPath();
$config->hasPathValidationConfig();
$config->pathValidationConfig();
$config->evaluationTime();
$config->targets();
$config->additionalCriticalExtensions();

docs.title: The path validation configuration
docs.text:
Pass a hardened one, since it governs the AC's own signature as well as the two paths:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathValidation\PathValidationConfig;

$pathConfig = PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig()
    ->withAllowedSignatureAlgorithms(...PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS)
    ->withMinimumRSAKeySize(PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE);

$config = $config->withPathValidationConfig($pathConfig);

The evaluation time is applied to the path configuration for you, so both paths and the AC are judged at the same instant.

The maximum path length is derived only when you supply no configuration

With no withPathValidationConfig(), the maximum length is taken from each path's own length. Once you supply a configuration, your withMaxLength() is respected — overriding it unconditionally made maxLength() a no-op for both paths.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Target\TargetGroup;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Target\TargetName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;

$config = $config->withTargets(
    TargetName::create(DNSName::create('app.example.com')),
    TargetGroup::create(DNSName::create('example.com'))
);

An AC with a targetInformation extension is refused unless one of its targets is among these. An AC without the extension is not targeted at all and passes whatever you configure — targeting constrains only the ACs that opt into it.

docs.title: Critical extensions
docs.text:
The validator processes targetInformation and noRevAvail. Anything else marked critical makes validation fail, which is RFC 5755 section 5 check 7: an attribute certificate carries authorisation, a critical extension is how its issuer narrows that authorisation, and honouring one you cannot process would grant the attributes unconditionally.

withAdditionalCriticalExtensions() stops the objection. It does not implement the check — that is yours.

docs.title: What the exception tells you
docs.text: Message Means Failed to validate holder PKC's certification path. the holder's path failed; $e->getPrevious() is the PathValidationException Name mismatch of AC's holder PKC. the path validated, but the AC is not held by that certificate Failed to validate issuer PKC's certification path. the issuer's path failed Name mismatch of AC's issuer PKC. the AC was not issued by that certificate Issuer PKC must not be a CA. the attribute authority's certificate asserts cA:TRUE Issuer PKC's Key Usage extension doesn't permit verification of digital signatures. neither digitalSignature nor nonRepudiation Issuer PKC is not a trusted attribute authority. not in the bundle you configured Signature algorithm … is not allowed. / RSA key size … is below the minimum … the AC's own signature, under the path policy Failed to verify signature. the AC's signature does not match Validity period has not started. / Attribute certificate has expired. the evaluation time Attribute certificate doesn't have a matching target. targetInformation does not include your targets Attribute certificate contains an unhandled critical extension: …. see above

docs.title: Using the result
docs.text:
$validated = ACValidator::create($ac, $config)->validate();

$attributes = $validated->acinfo()->attributes();

if ($attributes->hasRole()) {
    $role = $attributes->role()->roleName()->string();
}

The attributes are authorisation statements. Mapping them to permissions in your application is your decision, as is what to do when the same holder presents two attribute certificates that disagree.

And remember what the two paths do not tell you: revocation is not checked, for the holder's certificate, the issuer's, or — there being nothing to check it with — the attribute certificate itself.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
An X.509 certificate is a statement — this key belongs to this subject — and a signature over it. The library keeps the two apart, because that is what the structure does:

Certificate
├── TBSCertificate      the statement: version, serial, issuer, validity, subject, key, extensions
├── AlgorithmIdentifier how it was signed
└── Signature           the signature over the DER of the TBSCertificate

Certificate is immutable and read-only. Everything you build or change happens on TBSCertificate, and signing it produces a Certificate.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Certificate;

$certificate = Certificate::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('server.crt'));

$tbs = $certificate->tbsCertificate();
$tbs->subject()->toString();
$tbs->issuer()->toString();
$tbs->serialNumber();
$tbs->validity()->notAfter()->dateTime();
$tbs->subjectPublicKeyInfo();
$tbs->extensions();

docs.title: The three questions
docs.text:
They are different questions and the library answers them separately. Confusing them is the most common way to build something that looks safe and is not.

Question Call Is this certificate well-formed? it decoded: fromPEM(), fromDER() returned Was it signed by this key? $certificate->verify($publicKeyInfo) Does it chain to something I trust, in date, within its constraints? path validation

verify() takes the issuer's PublicKeyInfo and returns a boolean. It says nothing about trust, dates or constraints — only path validation does.

$certificate->verify($issuerCertificate->tbsCertificate()->subjectPublicKeyInfo());
$certificate->isSelfIssued();   // the subject and the issuer are the same name

Self-issued is not self-signed

isSelfIssued() compares the two names. It does not check the signature. A certificate whose subject and issuer match is self-signed only if it also verifies against its own key:

$selfSigned = $certificate->isSelfIssued()
    && $certificate->verify($certificate->tbsCertificate()->subjectPublicKeyInfo());

docs.title: Comparing two of them
docs.text:
$a->equals($b);                     // the two encodings, octet by octet
$a->hasEqualSubjectIdentity($b);    // same subject, same key, same serial number

hasEqualSubjectIdentity() is the looser question and not an identity check: two certificates can agree on all three and still be issued by different issuers with different extensions.

docs.title: In and out
docs.text:
Certificate::fromPEM($pem);
Certificate::fromDER($der);
Certificate::fromASN1($sequence);

$certificate->toPEM()->string();
$certificate->toDER();
$certificate->toASN1();
echo $certificate;              // the PEM block

A certificate read with fromDER() or fromPEM() keeps the TBSCertificate bytes exactly as they arrived, so verify() checks the signature over what the issuer signed rather than over what the parser produced. Re-encoding is not relied on for the one operation where a single differing octet would change the answer.

$certificate->toDER();   // the certificate as it was read

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Reading a certificate — every field, and what each one gives you.
  • Issuing a certificate — building a TBSCertificate and signing it.
  • Extensions — the twenty-odd extension classes.
  • Bundles and chains — holding several certificates: a trust store, a chain.

docs.title: Bundles and chains
docs.text:
Two collections, and the difference is not cosmetic.

Type Is Order CertificateBundle a set: a trust store, a pool of intermediates none CertificateChain a sequence: what a peer sent, end entity first significant

A bundle is something you assembled. A chain is something you were given. Keeping them apart is how the library stops a peer-supplied chain from being mistaken for a trust list; see Validating a path.

docs.title: CertificateBundle
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEMBundle;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;

$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::create($rootA, $rootB);
$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::fromPEMBundle(PEMBundle::fromFile('/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt'));
$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::fromPEMs(...$pems);

$trustAnchors = $trustAnchors->withCertificates($anotherRoot);
$trustAnchors = $trustAnchors->withPEM($pem);
$trustAnchors = $trustAnchors->withPEMBundle($pemBundle);

count($trustAnchors);
$trustAnchors->all();

foreach ($trustAnchors as $certificate) {
}

Immutable, like everything else: with*() returns a new bundle.

docs.title: Membership
docs.text:
$bundle->contains($certificate);

contains() is an exact question: it compares encodings octet by octet, through Certificate::equals(). Indexing by key identifier makes the lookup fast, but the answer is still an exact match.

It used to be looser, and that was a bug

The check was once on the serial number, the subject key identifier and the subject DN — three public values anyone can repeat. A certificate agreeing on those but differing in issuer, validity, every extension and the signature was reported as present, so contains() said yes for a certificate that was not in the bundle. If you need the looser grouping deliberately, ask Certificate::hasEqualSubjectIdentity() and know what it does not tell you.

docs.title: Lookup by key identifier
docs.text:
This is what path building uses to find an issuer:

$candidates = $bundle->allBySubjectKeyIdentifier($authorityKeyIdentifier);

A certificate is indexed twice: under the identifier computed from its public key, and under the one its subjectKeyIdentifier extension declares, when the two differ.

The declared value is arbitrary data that nothing checks against the key. Indexing on it alone meant that one certificate whose extension repeated a real intermediate's identifier could displace that intermediate and deny validation of a good chain. So the certificates whose computed identifier matches come first in the returned array, ahead of those that only claim the value — a caller that takes the first match takes the one that actually holds the key.

docs.title: CertificateChain
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateChain;

$chain = CertificateChain::create($leaf, $intermediate, $root);
$chain = CertificateChain::fromPEMs(...$pems);
$chain = CertificateChain::fromPEMString($pemText);

$chain->endEntityCertificate();     // the first
$chain->trustAnchorCertificate();   // the last
$chain->certificates();             // Certificate[], end entity first
count($chain);
echo $chain->toPEMString();

The order is end entity first, trust anchor last — the order TLS puts a chain on the wire. Both accessors throw LogicException on an empty chain.

trustAnchorCertificate() names a position, not a decision

It returns the last certificate of the chain, which on a chain from a peer is a certificate the peer chose. It is not a trust anchor in any sense that matters. Hence:

$path = $chain->certificationPath();           // or CertificationPath::fromCertificateChain($chain)
$path->validate($config);                      // throws: no trust anchor
$path->validate($config->withTrustAnchor($yourRoot));   // this is the question

A path built from a peer-supplied chain refuses to validate without an explicit anchor, by design.

docs.title: From one to the other
docs.text:
$path = $chain->certificationPath();   // a CertificationPath, reversed: anchor first

A CertificationPath runs the other way round — trust anchor first, target last — because that is the order RFC 5280's algorithm walks. The conversion reverses for you.

docs.title: Building a trust store
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEMBundle;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;

$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::fromPEMBundle(PEMBundle::fromFile('/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt'));

The library reads no system trust store of its own: there is no default list, and no discovery. Point it at a file your deployment controls, or assemble the bundle from the roots your application ships.

Count what a peer sends before you walk it; see Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
An extension is an OID, a critical flag and a value. The library parses twenty-odd of them into their own classes, and the critical flag is the first argument of every create().

$extensions = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->extensions();

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Extensions has a has*() and a getter for the extensions RFC 5280 defines:

$extensions->hasBasicConstraints();
$extensions->basicConstraints();          // LogicException if absent — ask first

$extensions->hasKeyUsage();
$extensions->hasExtendedKeyUsage();
$extensions->hasSubjectAlternativeName();
$extensions->hasIssuerAlternativeName();
$extensions->hasSubjectKeyIdentifier();
$extensions->hasAuthorityKeyIdentifier();
$extensions->hasNameConstraints();
$extensions->hasCertificatePolicies();
$extensions->hasPolicyMappings();
$extensions->hasPolicyConstraints();
$extensions->hasInhibitAnyPolicy();
$extensions->hasCRLDistributionPoints();

By OID, for anything:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Extension;

$extensions->has(Extension::OID_SUBJECT_INFORMATION_ACCESS);
$extension = $extensions->get(Extension::OID_SUBJECT_INFORMATION_ACCESS);

Or walk them all:

foreach ($extensions as $extension) {
    $extension->oid();
    $extension->isCritical();
    $extension->extensionName();   // a readable name, or the OID
}

Extension::OID_* names every extension of RFC 5280 and X.509, the obsolete ones included, prefixed OID_OBSOLETE_.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withAdditionalExtensions(
    BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false)
);

docs.title: Basic constraints
docs.text:
Is this a CA, and how many intermediates may follow it?

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\BasicConstraintsExtension;

BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false);       // critical, not a CA
BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, true);        // a CA, no path length limit
BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, true, 0);     // a CA that may issue only end entities

$extension->isCA();
$extension->hasPathLen();
$extension->pathLen();

Mark it critical. Path validation refuses a v3 intermediate without it, and refuses one whose cA is false.

docs.title: Key usage
docs.text:
A bit field. Combine the constants with |:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\KeyUsageExtension;

KeyUsageExtension::create(
    true,
    KeyUsageExtension::DIGITAL_SIGNATURE | KeyUsageExtension::KEY_ENCIPHERMENT
);

$extension->isDigitalSignature();
$extension->isNonRepudiation();
$extension->isKeyEncipherment();
$extension->isDataEncipherment();
$extension->isKeyAgreement();
$extension->isKeyCertSign();
$extension->isCRLSign();
$extension->isEncipherOnly();
$extension->isDecipherOnly();

KEY_CERT_SIGN is the one path validation looks at: an intermediate that has a keyUsage without it is refused.

docs.title: Extended key usage
docs.text:
What the key may be used for, as OIDs:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\ExtendedKeyUsageExtension;

ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::create(
    false,
    ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_SERVER_AUTH,
    ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_CLIENT_AUTH
);

$extension->has(ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_SERVER_AUTH);
$extension->purposes();
count($extension);

The constants cover TLS server and client authentication, code signing, email protection, time stamping, OCSP signing, the IPsec and EAP purposes, SSH client and server, and the CMC roles.

Path validation does not check extended key usage

RFC 5280's algorithm says nothing about it. Checking that a certificate is allowed to be a TLS server is a step of your own, after validation.

docs.title: Alternative names
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\IssuerAlternativeNameExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\SubjectAlternativeNameExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralNames;

SubjectAlternativeNameExtension::create(false, GeneralNames::create(
    DNSName::create('example.com'),
    DNSName::create('www.example.com')
));

$extension->names();    // GeneralNames

See General names. Mark subjectAltName critical when the subject DN is empty, as RFC 5280 requires — the validator handles a critical subjectAltName correctly either way.

docs.title: Key identifiers
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\AuthorityKeyIdentifierExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension;

SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension::create(false, $publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier());

AuthorityKeyIdentifierExtension::create(false, $caPublicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier());
AuthorityKeyIdentifierExtension::create(false, $keyId, $authorityCertIssuer, $authorityCertSerialNumber);

TBSCertificate::withIssuerCertificate() adds the authority key identifier for you, and fromCSR() adds the subject key identifier. These are what path building follows, so a CA that omits them makes its certificates harder to chain.

docs.title: Name constraints
docs.text:
What names an intermediate is allowed to vouch for. This is the extension that makes a delegated CA safe:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\NameConstraints\GeneralSubtree;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\NameConstraints\GeneralSubtrees;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\NameConstraintsExtension;

NameConstraintsExtension::create(
    true,
    GeneralSubtrees::create(GeneralSubtree::create(DNSName::create('example.com'))),
    GeneralSubtrees::create(GeneralSubtree::create(DNSName::create('internal.example.com')))
);

$extension->hasPermittedSubtrees();
$extension->permittedSubtrees();
$extension->hasExcludedSubtrees();
$extension->excludedSubtrees();

Path validation enforces these on DNS names, email addresses, URIs, IP addresses and directory names.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\CertificatePoliciesExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\CertificatePolicy\PolicyInformation;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\InhibitAnyPolicyExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\PolicyConstraintsExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\PolicyMappings\PolicyMapping;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\PolicyMappingsExtension;

CertificatePoliciesExtension::create(false, PolicyInformation::create('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.1'));
PolicyConstraintsExtension::create(true, 0, 0);          // requireExplicitPolicy, inhibitPolicyMapping
PolicyMappingsExtension::create(true, PolicyMapping::create($issuerPolicy, $subjectPolicy));
InhibitAnyPolicyExtension::create(true, 0);              // skipCerts

PolicyInformation::OID_ANY_POLICY is 2.5.29.32.0, the initial policy set of a default configuration. A PolicyInformation may carry qualifiers — CPSQualifier for a URI, UserNoticeQualifier for text. See Configuration.

docs.title: Distribution points and access descriptions
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\AccessDescription\AuthorityAccessDescription;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\AuthorityInformationAccessExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\CRLDistributionPointsExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\DistributionPoint\DistributionPoint;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\DistributionPoint\FullName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\UniformResourceIdentifier;

CRLDistributionPointsExtension::create(false, DistributionPoint::create(
    FullName::create(GeneralNames::create(UniformResourceIdentifier::create('http://crl.example.com/a.crl')))
));

AuthorityInformationAccessExtension::create(false, AuthorityAccessDescription::create(
    AuthorityAccessDescription::OID_METHOD_OSCP,
    UniformResourceIdentifier::create('http://ocsp.example.com/')
));

The library writes these and never follows them

It makes no network call: a CRL distribution point is not fetched and an OCSP responder is not asked. Reading them to drive your own revocation checking is exactly what they are for. See What validation does not do.

docs.title: The rest
docs.text: Class What it carries SubjectInformationAccessExtension where to find information about the subject SubjectDirectoryAttributesExtension X.501 attributes about the subject FreshestCRLExtension where to find the delta CRL NoRevocationAvailableExtension this certificate is not revocable (attribute certificates) TargetInformationExtension the targets an attribute certificate is meant for AAControlsExtension what an attribute authority may delegate

docs.title: An extension the library does not know
docs.text:
It becomes an UnknownExtension, which keeps the OID, the critical flag and the value as they were. Nothing is lost and nothing throws:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\UnknownExtension;

$extension = $extensions->get('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.7');

if ($extension instanceof UnknownExtension) {
    $der = $extension->extensionValue();       // the encoded value, as it arrived
    $element = Element::fromDER($der);         // decode it yourself
}

extensionValue() returns the raw DER of the extension's value, so what you do with it is the ASN.1 layer.

You can write one too:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\UTF8String;

UnknownExtension::create('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.7', false, UTF8String::create('whatever your schema says'));

A critical unknown extension makes a certificate useless

RFC 5280 says a validator must refuse a certificate carrying a critical extension it does not recognise, and this library's validator does. So:

  • do not sign one. TBSCertificate::fromCSR() never copies a critical UnknownExtension, whatever the allow list says, precisely because the result would be dead on arrival;
  • if your application processes one by its own means, tell the validator with PathValidationConfig::withAdditionalCriticalExtensions(). Naming it there means you check it — the validator only stops objecting.

docs.title: Issuing a certificate
docs.text: TBSCertificate is the mutable-by-copy builder, sign() turns it into a Certificate.

docs.title: The shortest complete example
docs.text:
A self-signed certificate, which is a certificate whose issuer is its own subject:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature\SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PrivateKeyInfo;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\TBSCertificate;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Validity;

$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('key.pem'));
$name = Name::fromString('cn=example.com, o=ACME Ltd, c=FR');

$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::create(
    $name,                              // subject
    $privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo(),   // the subject's public key
    $name,                              // issuer
    Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 1 year')
);

$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign(
    SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(),
    $privateKeyInfo
);

file_put_contents('cert.pem', $certificate->toPEM()->string());

Note the argument order of create(): subject, key, issuer, validity. The subject comes first.

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Time;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Validity;

Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 90 days');
Validity::fromStrings('2026-01-01 00:00:00', '2027-01-01 00:00:00', 'UTC');

Validity::create(
    Time::create(new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-01', new DateTimeZone('UTC'))),
    Time::create(new DateTimeImmutable('2027-01-01', new DateTimeZone('UTC')))
);

The strings go through DateTimeImmutable, so anything it understands works. Time picks UTCTime before 2050 and GeneralizedTime after, as RFC 5280 asks.

docs.title: The serial number
docs.text:
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withRandomSerialNumber();      // 20 octets
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withRandomSerialNumber(16);
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withSerialNumber('12345');     // if you keep a register

Leaving it unset is safe: sign() draws a 20-octet random serial number — DEFAULT_RANDOM_SERIAL_SIZE, the RFC 5280 maximum — rather than writing a zero.

A constant serial number breaks two things at once

It removes the unpredictability that protects issuance against collision attacks, and it breaks CRL revocation, which identifies a certificate by the (issuer, serial number) pair. If you draw your own, use at least TBSCertificate::MIN_RANDOM_SERIAL_SIZE — nine octets. That is the 64 bits of CSPRNG output the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements ask for, plus the octet the sign bit costs. A smaller size still works and raises a deprecation notice saying how many bits it actually carries.

docs.title: The version
docs.text: You do not set it. sign() works out the minimum the structure needs: version 3 when there are extensions, version 2 when there is a unique identifier, version 1 otherwise. withVersion() exists if you need to force one.

docs.title: Signing as a CA
docs.text:
withIssuerCertificate() fills in what the issuer's certificate implies — the issuer DN from the CA's subject, and an authorityKeyIdentifier pointing at the CA's key:

$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::create(
    $subjectName,
    $subjectPublicKeyInfo,
    Name::create(),                       // replaced below
    Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 90 days')
);

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate
    ->withIssuerCertificate($caCertificate)
    ->withRandomSerialNumber();

$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign(
    SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(),
    $caPrivateKeyInfo                     // the CA's key, not the subject's
);

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Two methods, and the difference matters:

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withExtensions($extensions);          // replaces the whole set
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withAdditionalExtensions(...$exts);   // adds to it

withExtensions() after withIssuerCertificate() throws away the authorityKeyIdentifier that call added. Use withAdditionalExtensions(), or set the extensions first.

A typical TLS server certificate:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\BasicConstraintsExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\ExtendedKeyUsageExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\KeyUsageExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\SubjectAlternativeNameExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralNames;

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withAdditionalExtensions(
    BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false),
    KeyUsageExtension::create(true, KeyUsageExtension::DIGITAL_SIGNATURE | KeyUsageExtension::KEY_ENCIPHERMENT),
    ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::create(false, ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_SERVER_AUTH),
    SubjectAlternativeNameExtension::create(false, GeneralNames::create(
        DNSName::create('example.com'),
        DNSName::create('www.example.com')
    )),
    SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension::create(false, $subjectPublicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier())
);

A CA certificate instead:

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withAdditionalExtensions(
    BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, true, 0),   // critical, cA, pathLenConstraint
    KeyUsageExtension::create(true, KeyUsageExtension::KEY_CERT_SIGN | KeyUsageExtension::CRL_SIGN)
);

The first argument of every extension is $critical. See Extensions for the whole set.

A CA certificate without basicConstraints is not a CA

Path validation refuses an intermediate that does not assert cA:TRUE, and refuses one whose keyUsage omits keyCertSign when it has a keyUsage at all. Setting both is not a formality.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign($algorithm, $privateKeyInfo);
$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign($algorithm, $privateKeyInfo, $crypto);

The algorithm has to match the key: SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier for an RSA key, ECDSAWithSHA256AlgorithmIdentifier for an EC key, Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier for an Ed25519 key. A mismatch raises UnexpectedValueException naming both.

Signing sets the signature field inside the signed part and repeats the algorithm outside, so the two agree — which is what Certificate::fromASN1() checks when the certificate is read back.

sign() returns a new Certificate and leaves the TBSCertificate untouched; nothing in the library mutates.

docs.title: Checking what you made
docs.text:
$certificate->verify($privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo());       // the signature is good
$certificate->tbsCertificate()->version();                    // 2, i.e. v3
echo $certificate->toPEM()->string();

And against OpenSSL, which is worth doing once for any new issuance path:

openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text

docs.title: From a certification request
docs.text: When the subject sent a CSR, start from it — but treat it as untrusted input. See Issuing from a request, which is the page to read before you wire an issuance endpoint to anything.

docs.title: Reading a certificate
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Certificate;

$certificate = Certificate::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('server.crt'));
$tbs = $certificate->tbsCertificate();

Everything below is on $tbs, except the three fields of the outer structure.

docs.title: The outer structure
docs.text:
$certificate->signatureAlgorithm();   // a SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier
$certificate->signatureValue();       // a Signature
$certificate->tbsCertificate();       // the signed part

The signature algorithm appears twice in a certificate — once outside, once inside the signed part — and they have to agree. fromASN1() checks that the OIDs match and refuses the certificate otherwise, which closes the oldest trick in the format.

Only the OIDs are compared

For RSASSA-PSS the parameters matter as much as the OID — a hash, MGF and salt length downgrade would slip through an OID-only comparison — which is one reason PSS is not implemented and a PSS-signed certificate is refused outright.

docs.title: Version, serial number
docs.text:
$tbs->version();          // 0, 1 or 2 for v1, v2, v3
$tbs->hasVersion();
$tbs->serialNumber();     // a decimal string
$tbs->hasSerialNumber();

The constants are TBSCertificate::VERSION_1, VERSION_2 and VERSION_3, whose values are 0, 1 and 2: the field is zero-based, as the ASN.1 says. Almost everything you will meet is a v3 certificate.

The serial number is a decimal string, not an integer. A 20-octet serial number does not fit in a PHP integer, and comparing serial numbers as integers is how revocation lookups break.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
$tbs->subject();   // a Name
$tbs->issuer();    // a Name

$tbs->subject()->toString();
$tbs->subject()->firstValueOf('cn')->stringValue();

See Distinguished names. For a TLS certificate the hostname is in subjectAltName, not in the common name.

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
$validity = $tbs->validity();

$notBefore = $validity->notBefore()->dateTime();   // DateTimeImmutable
$notAfter = $validity->notAfter()->dateTime();

$now = new DateTimeImmutable();
$inDate = $now >= $notBefore && $now <= $notAfter;

Time wraps a DateTimeImmutable and remembers which ASN.1 type it was read from — UTCTime before 2050, GeneralizedTime after — so a round trip gives back the same bytes.

Checking the dates yourself is not validation

A certificate in date may still be revoked, outside its constraints, or signed by a key you have no reason to trust. Path validation checks the dates of every certificate in the path against one reference time; see Validating a path.

docs.title: The public key
docs.text:
$publicKeyInfo = $tbs->subjectPublicKeyInfo();

$publicKeyInfo->algorithmIdentifier()->name();
$publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier();        // 20 bytes, RFC 5280 method 1
$publicKeyInfo->publicKey();            // RSAPublicKey, ECPublicKey, …

See Public keys.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
$extensions = $tbs->extensions();

$extensions->hasBasicConstraints();
$extensions->basicConstraints()->isCA();

$extensions->hasSubjectAlternativeName();
$extensions->subjectAlternativeName()->names()->firstDNS();

count($extensions);

foreach ($extensions as $extension) {
    $extension->oid();
    $extension->isCritical();
    $extension->extensionName();
}

Every extension in the certificate is there, known or not. See Extensions.

docs.title: Unique identifiers
docs.text:
Two fields from version 2, which you will almost certainly never meet:

$tbs->hasIssuerUniqueID();
$tbs->issuerUniqueID()->string();
$tbs->hasSubjectUniqueID();
$tbs->subjectUniqueID()->string();

They exist to disambiguate a reused name. RFC 5280 says not to issue new certificates with them.

docs.title: Printing one
docs.text:
There is no formatter in the library — no openssl x509 -text equivalent — so a dump is a few lines of your own:

$tbs = $certificate->tbsCertificate();

printf(
    "subject:  %s\nissuer:   %s\nserial:   %s\nvalid:    %s → %s\nkey:      %s\nalgorithm: %s\n",
    $tbs->subject()->toString(),
    $tbs->issuer()->toString(),
    $tbs->serialNumber(),
    $tbs->validity()->notBefore()->dateTime()->format('c'),
    $tbs->validity()->notAfter()->dateTime()->format('c'),
    $tbs->subjectPublicKeyInfo()->algorithmIdentifier()->name(),
    $certificate->signatureAlgorithm()->name()
);

foreach ($tbs->extensions() as $extension) {
    printf("  %-28s %s%s\n", $extension->extensionName(), $extension->oid(), $extension->isCritical() ? ' (critical)' : '');
}

docs.title: What can go wrong
docs.text:
Thrown When UnexpectedValueException the PEM label is not CERTIFICATE DecodeException the DER is malformed, nested too deep, or carries a repeated optional field UnexpectedValueException the outer and inner signature algorithms disagree, or the signature algorithm is one the library refuses LogicException you asked for a field the certificate does not have — call the matching has*() first

Material from a peer deserves the limits in Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: Certification paths
docs.text:
A certification path is a sequence of certificates running from a trust anchor to a target, each one signed by the one before it.

CertificationPath
  [0] the trust anchor         a certificate YOU chose
  [1] an intermediate
  [2] …
  [n] the target              the end-entity certificate you are asking about

Note the direction. A TLS chain on the wire runs the other way — end entity first — which is what CertificateChain models. A CertificationPath is reversed because that is the order RFC 5280's algorithm walks.

docs.title: Two halves of the problem
docs.text:
Building is finding a path: given a target and a bundle of certificates you trust, work out a sequence that leads from one to the other. See Building a path.

Validating is checking it: signatures, dates, constraints, policies. See Validating a path.

Building a path does not validate it, and validating one does not require you to have built it. The usual code does both, in that order:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\CertificationPath;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\Exception\PathValidationException;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathValidation\PathValidationConfig;

$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::create($rootA, $rootB);              // your trust store
$intermediates = CertificateBundle::create(...$chainFromPeer);          // untrusted, bridges the path

$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($leafFromPeer, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);

try {
    $result = $path->validate(PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig());
} catch (PathValidationException $e) {
    // the chain does not lead to any certificate you trust
}

That is the shape to copy. toTarget() starts from the trust list you gave it, so the path it returns is already headed by a certificate you chose.

docs.title: The four ways to get a path
docs.text:
Factory Head of the path Needs an explicit anchor to validate? toTarget($target, $trustAnchors, $intermediates) from your trust list no fromTrustAnchorToTarget($anchor, $target, $intermediates) the anchor you named no create(...$certificates) whatever you passed first yes in practice — a deprecation notice without one fromCertificateChain($chain) whatever the peer sent first yes — throws without one

create() is the constructor an integrator reaches for first, and it is the one that cannot tell a path anchored in your trust store from one anchored in an attacker's. Prefer toTarget().

docs.title: Reading a path
docs.text:
$path->certificates();              // Certificate[], anchor first
$path->trustAnchorCertificate();    // the first
$path->endEntityCertificate();      // the last
$path->certificateChain();          // a CertificateChain, reversed
$path->startsWith($rootA);          // does it begin with these certificates?
count($path);

foreach ($path as $certificate) {
}

startsWith() is the cheap check that a path begins where you expect — useful when you hold several anchors and want to know which one a built path used.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Building a path — how an issuer is found, and the bounds on the search.
  • Validating a path — the algorithm, the result, the exceptions.
  • Configuration — every knob of PathValidationConfig, and the ones to turn.
  • What validation does not do — read this before you rely on a successful validation.

docs.title: Building a path
docs.text: Path building answers: given this certificate, and these certificates I trust, is there a chain between them?

docs.title: The usual call
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\CertificationPath;

$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($target, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);
  • $trustAnchors is a bundle you assembled. The path will be headed by one of its certificates.
  • $intermediates is the pool to bridge the gap, typically what the peer sent. It is untrusted: a certificate from it can appear in the middle of a path, never at its head.

docs.title: The builder directly
docs.text:
toTarget() is a shortcut for the shortest path. When more than one path exists, you may want them all:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathBuilding\CertificationPathBuilder;

$builder = CertificationPathBuilder::create($trustAnchors);

$paths = $builder->allPathsToTarget($target, $intermediates);   // CertificationPath[]
$path = $builder->shortestPathToTarget($target, $intermediates);

The shortest path is not necessarily the valid one

A short path may fail validation — an expired intermediate, a name constraint, a policy — where a longer one would succeed. shortestPathToTarget() commits to one. When more than one path is possible, take allPathsToTarget() and validate them in turn:

foreach ($builder->allPathsToTarget($target, $intermediates) as $path) {
    try {
        return $path->validate($config);
    } catch (PathValidationException) {
        continue;
    }
}
throw new RuntimeException('No path validates.');

Among paths of equal length the order is deterministic, so shortestPathToTarget() returns the same path for the same input.

docs.title: How an issuer is found
docs.text:
For each certificate, the builder looks for candidates that could have issued it:

  1. By authority key identifier. If the certificate has an authorityKeyIdentifier with a key identifier, candidates come from allBySubjectKeyIdentifier() on the bundle. That lookup puts the certificates whose identifier is computed from their key ahead of those that merely declare the value in an extension — a declared identifier is arbitrary data that nothing checks against the key.
  2. By name, as a fallback. When that yields nothing, every certificate in the bundle is a candidate. RFC 5280 requires the authority key identifier on a CA-issued certificate, but plenty of real certificates omit it, and the issuer name identifies the issuer on its own. RFC 4158 section 3.5.12 expects a builder to match on the name. Without this fallback such a certificate could never be chained, which would push integrators towards the unsafe constructor.
  3. Then by name, always. Every candidate must have a subject DN equal to the target's issuer DN, with the X.501 comparison rules — not a string comparison.

Building matches names and follows identifiers. It does not verify signatures: that is validation's job, and a built path is a hypothesis until you validate it.

docs.title: The bounds on the search
docs.text:
The search runs over certificates a peer chose, so it is bounded three ways:

Bound Value Why Path length while resolving 10 certificates bounds the depth, on top of loop detection Paths produced in one step 100 a bundle of mutually compatible certificates yields an exponential number of paths even with no loop Certificates examined 1000 work has to be counted where it is done: a subtree that returns no path has still explored itself, and a bundle chaining to no anchor is exactly that shape

Exceeding one raises PathBuildingException. A self-issued certificate is not followed as an intermediate, and a certificate already on the path being resolved is not revisited.

These bounds are not configurable. They are a cap on attacker-controlled work, not a tuning parameter.

docs.title: When nothing is found
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\Exception\PathBuildingException;

try {
    $path = CertificationPath::toTarget($target, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);
} catch (PathBuildingException $e) {
    // no path, or the search hit a bound
}

PathBuildingException also wraps a name that cannot be prepared for comparison: matching an issuer name is a name comparison, and a string the X.520 preparation steps refuse stops the resolution rather than being reported as "not equal". It is reported as a building failure like any other, with the original as its previous.

Common causes of no path at all:

  • the peer sent a leaf without its intermediates, and your pool has none;
  • your trust store does not hold the root the chain leads to;
  • an intermediate's subject DN does not match what the leaf names as its issuer.

docs.title: Holding a path you already have
docs.text:
When you already know the sequence — from a configuration file, from a chain a peer sent — you do not need the builder:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\CertificationPath;

$path = CertificationPath::create($root, $intermediate, $leaf);       // anchor first
$path = CertificationPath::fromCertificateChain($chainFromPeer);      // reverses it for you

Both of these need an explicit trust anchor to validate

Neither knows where its first certificate came from. fromCertificateChain() throws without withTrustAnchor(), because a peer decided what its first certificate is. create() raises a deprecation notice and falls back to its first certificate, and that fallback will be removed. See Validating a path.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
PathValidationConfig is immutable: every with*() returns a copy.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathValidation\PathValidationConfig;

$config = PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig();                        // now, maximum length 3
$config = PathValidationConfig::create(new DateTimeImmutable(), 5);     // reference time, maximum length

docs.title: What a hardened configuration looks like
docs.text:
$config = PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig()
    ->withAllowedSignatureAlgorithms(...PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS)
    ->withMinimumRSAKeySize(PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE)
    ->withTrustAnchor($root);

Two settings, and they are the two whose defaults are looser than a new deployment would choose.

docs.title: The trust anchor
docs.text:
$config = $config->withTrustAnchor($root);

$config->hasTrustAnchor();
$config->trustAnchor();

The single most important setting. See Validating a path.

docs.title: Allowed signature algorithms
docs.text:
$config = $config->withAllowedSignatureAlgorithms(...$oids);
$config->allowedSignatureAlgorithms();

Replaces the set entirely — it is not additive.

Constant Contains DEFAULT_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS SHA-1 through SHA-512 with RSA, ECDSA with the same hashes, Ed25519, Ed448 HARDENED_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS the same without SHA-1
