MD2, MD4 and MD5 are in neither: chosen-prefix collisions against MD5 have been practical since 2009, which is enough to forge a certificate that verifies, and no authority in service still signs with them. Refusing them costs nothing, and an opt-in would protect only those who already knew to ask.

SHA-1 is in the default, despite chosen-prefix collisions against it being practical since 2020. Legacy enterprise and device PKIs continue to rely on it, and cutting them off silently in a patch release is not this library's call. If yours is not one of them, harden it. HARDENED_… is the set the default will narrow to in a future major release.

RSASSA-PSS is in neither, because it is not implemented: a PSS-signed certificate is refused when it is parsed, so allowing the OID would advertise a capability that does not exist.

An algorithm not in the set is refused before the signature is checked — a signature is only as good as its digest, and without the check the validator would accept MD5 with no way for the application to say no.

Ed25519 and Ed448 are allowed by default but may not be checkable

Whether they can be verified depends on the runtime. Probe with OpenSSLCrypto::supportsSignatureAlgorithm() and narrow the set rather than letting a chain fail closed; see The crypto engine.

docs.title: The RSA floor
docs.text:
$config = $config->withMinimumRSAKeySize(2048);
$config->minimumRSAKeySize();
Constant Bits DEFAULT_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE 1024 HARDENED_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE 2048

RSA-512 has been factorable for decades and RSA-768 was factored in 2009, so a signature made with such a key proves nothing and the default refuses them. It stops at 1024 rather than at the 2048 bits the CA/Browser Forum has required since 2014, for the same reason SHA-1 stays in the default set.

Zero disables the check; a negative value raises InvalidArgumentException.

Only RSA is covered: an EC key's strength is fixed by its named curve, and the curves this library knows are all above the line.

docs.title: Reference time
docs.text:
$config = $config->withDateTime(new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-01'));
$config->dateTime();

Every validity period in the path is checked against this one instant. Setting it to the past is how you validate a signature that was made when the certificate was still valid; setting it from a request parameter is how you let a peer validate an expired chain.

docs.title: Maximum path length
docs.text:
$config = $config->withMaxLength(5);
$config->maxLength();

The default is 3. It bounds the path independently of any pathLenConstraint, and the lower of the two wins.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
$config = $config->withPolicySet('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.1', '1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.2');
$config = $config->withExplicitPolicy(true);
$config = $config->withPolicyMappingInhibit(true);
$config = $config->withAnyPolicyInhibit(true);

$config->policySet();
$config->explicitPolicy();
$config->policyMappingInhibit();
$config->anyPolicyInhibit();
Setting Default Means withPolicySet() [PolicyInformation::OID_ANY_POLICY] the initial policy set: which policies you accept withExplicitPolicy() false the path must be valid for at least one policy of that set withPolicyMappingInhibit() false refuse policy mapping along the path withAnyPolicyInhibit() false refuse anyPolicy

Most deployments leave all four alone: policy processing matters inside a PKI that defines policies and cross-certifies, and a web PKI client has no use for it. If you set withPolicySet() to a specific OID, set withExplicitPolicy(true) as well — otherwise a path valid for no policy at all still passes.

A failure here reads No valid policies.

docs.title: Critical extensions you handle yourself
docs.text:
$config = $config->withAdditionalCriticalExtensions('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.7');
$config->additionalCriticalExtensions();

Validation refuses any certificate carrying a critical extension it cannot process. Declaring an OID here stops that rejection.

Naming an extension here means you check it

The validator stops objecting; it does not start handling. An OID listed here with no code behind it is a critical extension nobody enforces, which is exactly what the critical flag exists to prevent.

docs.title: Version 1 and version 2 intermediates
docs.text:
$config = $config->withLegacyV1IntermediatesTrusted(true);
$config->legacyV1IntermediatesTrusted();

Default false, and leave it there.

What this flag actually allows

A v1 or v2 certificate carries no extensions, hence neither basicConstraints nor keyUsage, so nothing in it states that it may sign certificates. RFC 5280 section 6.1.4 (k) requires the application to confirm that out of band or reject it.

Turning this on means any end-entity certificate a trusted CA ever issued in version 1 becomes usable as an intermediate CA for any identity. Set it only for certificates vouched for by other means, never to make a chain you do not understand go through.

docs.title: Everything at a glance
docs.text: Setting Default Change it? withTrustAnchor() none yes, unless the path came from toTarget() withAllowedSignatureAlgorithms() includes SHA-1 yes, if you can refuse SHA-1 withMinimumRSAKeySize() 1024 yes, if you can require 2048 withDateTime() now only to validate at another instant withMaxLength() 3 if your PKI is deeper withPolicySet() and the policy flags anyPolicy, all off only in a PKI that defines policies withAdditionalCriticalExtensions() empty only for extensions you really process withLegacyV1IntermediatesTrusted() false almost never

docs.title: Validating a path
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\Exception\PathValidationException;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathValidation\PathValidationConfig;

try {
    $result = $path->validate(PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig());
} catch (PathValidationException $e) {
    // the path does not validate; $e->getMessage() says why
}

Validation either returns a PathValidationResult or throws. There is no boolean and no partial success.

docs.title: The trust anchor is an input
docs.text:
This is the one thing to get right. The trust anchor is something your application names, never something read out of the material a peer sent.

// Right: the path is headed by a certificate from your own trust list.
$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($leafFromPeer, $trustAnchors, $intermediatesFromPeer);
$result = $path->validate(PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig());

// Right: you hold the path, so you name the anchor.
$config = PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig()->withTrustAnchor($root);
$result = $path->validate($config);

Left to itself, validation falls back to the first certificate of the path and then confirms only that the chain is internally consistent — which any attacker can arrange with a root of their own.

The library makes that hard to do by accident:

Path from Without withTrustAnchor() toTarget(), fromTrustAnchorToTarget() fine: already headed by a certificate from the trust list you gave fromCertificateChain() throws. A peer decided what the first certificate is create() deprecation notice, then falls back to the first certificate. The fallback will be removed in the next major release

Nothing in a PathValidationResult distinguishes a chain anchored in your trust store from one anchored in an attacker's, which is why the warning is at the call rather than in the result. Use the deprecation notice to find your create() call sites.

docs.title: What validation checks
docs.text:
The algorithm is RFC 5280 section 6.1, walked from the anchor to the target.

Per certificate

  • the signature algorithm is in the allowed set — an algorithm not named is refused before the signature is even checked, because a signature is only as good as its digest;
  • the issuer's RSA modulus is at or above the minimum key size;
  • the signature verifies against the working public key;
  • the validity period contains the reference time;
  • the issuer DN equals the previous certificate's subject DN, under the X.501 rules;
  • no name of the certificate falls outside the permitted subtrees or inside the excluded subtrees of the name constraints in force;
  • every critical extension is one the validator recognises, or one you declared with withAdditionalCriticalExtensions().

Per intermediate, additionally

  • it is a v3 certificate carrying basicConstraints with cA:TRUE — a v1 or v2 certificate is refused unless you set withLegacyV1IntermediatesTrusted(true);
  • its keyUsage, if it has one, includes keyCertSign;
  • the remaining path length has not run out, counting both the configured maximum and every pathLenConstraint met along the way.

Across the path

  • the policy tree: certificate policies, policy mappings, requireExplicitPolicy, inhibitPolicyMapping and inhibitAnyPolicy, intersected with the initial policy set.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
$result = $path->validate($config);

$result->certificate();         // the end-entity certificate
$result->getPublicKeyInfo();    // its public key, as validation worked it out
$result->getPublicKeyAlgo();
$result->getPublicKeyParameters();
$result->policies();            // the policies valid for this path
$result->getPolicyTree();       // the tree, or null

getPublicKeyInfo() is the useful one: the key you may now rely on, carried forward through the path including any inherited parameters.

docs.title: Using your own crypto engine
docs.text:
$result = $path->validate($config, $crypto);

See The crypto engine.

docs.title: What the exception tells you
docs.text:
Everything raises PathValidationException, with a message naming the check that failed:

Message Means Signature algorithm … is not allowed. not in the configured set — SHA-1 if you hardened, MD5 always RSA key size … is below the minimum of … bits. the issuer's modulus is too small Certificate signature doesn't match. the signature is wrong Failed to verify signature: … the engine could not ask — often EdDSA on a runtime without it Certificate has expired. / … has not started. the reference time is outside a validity period Certification issuer mismatch. a subject DN and the next issuer DN do not match Certificate is not a CA certificate. / v3 certificate must have basicConstraints extension. an intermediate that is not one keyCertSign usage not set. an intermediate whose keyUsage forbids signing certificates Certification path length exceeded. the configured maximum, or a pathLenConstraint Name '…' is not within the permitted subtrees. / … is within an excluded subtree. name constraints No valid policies. the policy tree is empty and an explicit policy was required Certificate contains an unhandled critical extension: …. a critical extension nobody processes A name of the certification path cannot be prepared for comparison: … see below

A name that cannot be compared fails validation

A name comparison here is a security decision, so a string the X.520 preparation steps refuse fails the validation rather than being reported as "not equal" — which would let a name escape an excluded subtree. It is reported as a PathValidationException with the original as its previous, instead of escaping as the StringPreparationException raised deep inside the comparison.

docs.title: Trying several paths
docs.text:
When more than one path exists, a failure on one says nothing about the others:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathBuilding\CertificationPathBuilder;

$builder = CertificationPathBuilder::create($trustAnchors);

foreach ($builder->allPathsToTarget($target, $intermediates) as $candidate) {
    try {
        $result = $candidate->validate($config);
        break;
    } catch (PathValidationException) {
        continue;
    }
}

docs.title: Then what
docs.text:
A successful validation is a strong statement with sharp edges. It does not mean the certificate is unrevoked, that it is the right certificate for the host you dialled, or that its extended key usage allows what you are about to do.

What validation does not do is the other half of this page.

docs.title: What validation does not do
docs.text:
A successful validate() is a precise statement: this chain is well-formed, every signature holds, every certificate was in date at the reference instant, the constraints along the path are satisfied, and it leads to the anchor you named.

That is less than "this certificate is good". The gap is this page.

docs.title: Revocation is not checked
docs.text:
A revoked certificate validates. The library has no CRL parser and no OCSP client, and it never opens a network connection — nothing is fetched from an authorityInformationAccess extension or a CRL distribution point.

This is by design, not an omission waiting for a release. Revocation checking is the calling application's responsibility.

What the library gives you to do it with:

$extensions = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->extensions();

if ($extensions->hasCRLDistributionPoints()) {
    foreach ($extensions->crlDistributionPoints()->distributionPoints() as $point) {
        // the URIs are in $point->fullName(), fetch and check them yourself
    }
}

if ($extensions->has(Extension::OID_AUTHORITY_INFORMATION_ACCESS)) {
    // AuthorityAccessDescription::OID_METHOD_OSCP gives the responder's URI
}

And what identifies a certificate to a CRL: the (issuer, serial number) pair.

$tbs = $certificate->tbsCertificate();
$key = [$tbs->issuer()->toString(), $tbs->serialNumber()];

The serial number is a decimal string. Comparing serial numbers as PHP integers is how revocation lookups silently stop matching.

docs.title: No hostname, no identity matching
docs.text:
Path validation never looks at a hostname. It does not know you dialled example.com.

$names = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->extensions()->subjectAlternativeName()->names();
$names->firstDNS();   // what the issuer wrote

Deciding whether that names the server you meant to reach — wildcards, trailing dots, internationalised domains, whether to look at the common name at all, the rules of the protocol you are speaking — is a step of your own. The same goes for matching an email address in an S/MIME certificate, or a user identifier in a client certificate.

docs.title: Extended key usage is not checked
docs.text:
RFC 5280's algorithm says nothing about extKeyUsage, so neither does the validator. A certificate issued for email protection validates perfectly well as the far end of a TLS chain.

$extensions = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->extensions();

if (! $extensions->hasExtendedKeyUsage()
    || ! $extensions->extendedKeyUsage()->has(ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_SERVER_AUTH)) {
    throw new RuntimeException('Not a TLS server certificate.');
}

keyUsage on the end-entity certificate is likewise yours to check: the validator enforces it on intermediates — keyCertSign — not on the leaf.

docs.title: No system trust store
docs.text:
There is no default list of roots, and nothing reads the operating system's. Everything you trust, you hand over:

$trustAnchors = CertificateBundle::fromPEMBundle(PEMBundle::fromFile('/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt'));

That is a feature — the trust decision is visible in your code — and it means an empty bundle validates nothing rather than falling back to something broad.

docs.title: Attribute certificates need their authorities named
docs.text: ACValidator does not implement RFC 5755 section 5 check 4 on its own. Without ACValidationConfig::withTrustedAttributeAuthorities(), it accepts whatever end-entity certificate the issuer path ends in. See Validating an attribute certificate.

docs.title: RSASSA-PSS is refused, not validated
docs.text: A PSS-signed certificate is refused when it is parsed, so it never reaches validation. If your PKI uses PSS, this library cannot verify its certificates — and the OID is deliberately absent from the allowed set so that nothing pretends otherwise.

docs.title: EdDSA may fail for the wrong reason
docs.text: Ed25519 and Ed448 are allowed by default, but verification depends on the extensions loaded. On a runtime without EdDSA the chain fails closed, and Failed to verify signature: … is indistinguishable from a bad signature. Probe at boot; see The crypto engine.

docs.title: Nothing bounds the input for you
docs.text: The decoder caps nesting depth. It does not cap the size of the string you hand it, or the number of certificates in a bundle you walk. See Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: The checklist
docs.text:
For a TLS client, after a successful validation:

  • [ ] revocation checked, by CRL or OCSP, with your own code;
  • [ ] the hostname matched against subjectAltName, with the rules of your protocol;
  • [ ] extKeyUsage includes the purpose you are about to use the certificate for;
  • [ ] keyUsage on the leaf permits what you are about to do;
  • [ ] the configuration was hardened if your deployment can refuse SHA-1 and 1024-bit RSA;
  • [ ] the trust anchor came from your trust store, not from the path.

If you are implementing TLS itself, note that the protocol has more requirements than RFC 5280 does. This library gives you the certificate layer; it is not a TLS stack.

docs.title: Certification requests
docs.text:
A certification request — a CSR, after RFC 2986 — is a subject saying here is my public key, here is the name I would like, please issue me a certificate, signed with the matching private key.

CertificationRequest
├── CertificationRequestInfo    version, subject, public key, attributes
├── AlgorithmIdentifier         how it was signed
└── Signature                   over the DER of the CertificationRequestInfo

Same split as a certificate: CertificationRequestInfo is the builder, CertificationRequest is the signed result.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationRequest\CertificationRequest;

$csr = CertificationRequest::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('request.csr'));

$cri = $csr->certificationRequestInfo();
$cri->subject()->toString();
$cri->subjectPKInfo();
$csr->signatureAlgorithm()->name();

docs.title: What a request proves, and what it does not
docs.text:
A valid signature on a CSR proves one thing: whoever produced it holds the private key matching the public key inside. That is a proof of possession, and it is useful.

It does not prove that the subject is entitled to the name it asked for, that the extensions it requested are ones it should get, or that anyone should issue it anything. Every field of a request was chosen by whoever submitted it.

Read this before you wire a request to an issuance path

Issuing from a request is where that matters. TBSCertificate::fromCSR() does not verify the signature, and the extensions a certificate may do things with are never copied from a request.

docs.title: Verifying a request
docs.text:
if (! $csr->verify()) {
    throw new RuntimeException('The request is not signed by the key it carries.');
}

verify() takes no key: a request is self-signed by definition, so the key it checks against is the one inside it. Pass a crypto engine as the only argument to use your own.

It returns false rather than throwing for anything that means the signature was not verified: an algorithm the runtime cannot check, a key the algorithm does not match, an engine failure. The algorithm is named by the request, so an attacker picks it, and if (! $csr->verify()) in your code must not become an unhandled fatal.

A request read from bytes is verified over those bytes

fromDER() and fromPEM() keep the CertificationRequestInfo exactly as it arrived, so the signature is checked over what the subject signed. A request you built in memory was never received as bytes, and re-encoding it is then the only option — and the correct one.

docs.title: In and out
docs.text:
CertificationRequest::fromPEM($pem);      // label: CERTIFICATE REQUEST
CertificationRequest::fromDER($der);
CertificationRequest::fromASN1($sequence);

$csr->toPEM()->string();
$csr->toDER();
$csr->toASN1();
echo $csr;

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
A request carries attributes, and the one that matters is the extension request:

$cri = $csr->certificationRequestInfo();

if ($cri->hasAttributes() && $cri->attributes()->hasExtensionRequest()) {
    $requested = $cri->attributes()->extensionRequest()->extensions();

    foreach ($requested as $extension) {
        $extension->oid();
        $extension->isCritical();
    }
}

attributes() throws LogicException when there are none, so ask hasAttributes() first. The collection is a SetOfAttributes; see Attributes.

These are requests, not facts. Reading them tells you what the subject asked for. Deciding what to honour is the issuer's job.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Creating a request — building and signing one, as the subject.
  • Issuing from a request — turning one into a certificate, as the issuer.

docs.title: Creating a request
docs.text: This is the subject's side: you hold a key, you want a certificate for it.

docs.title: The whole thing
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature\SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PrivateKeyInfo;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationRequest\CertificationRequestInfo;

$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('key.pem'));

$cri = CertificationRequestInfo::create(
    Name::fromString('cn=example.com, o=ACME Ltd, c=FR'),
    $privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo()
);

$csr = $cri->sign(SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(), $privateKeyInfo);

file_put_contents('request.csr', $csr->toPEM()->string());

The key you sign with must be the one whose public half you put in: that is the proof of possession the request exists to carry. The algorithm has to match the key — ECDSAWithSHA256AlgorithmIdentifier for an EC key, Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier for an Ed25519 key — and a mismatch raises UnexpectedValueException.

sign() takes a crypto engine as an optional third argument.

docs.title: Requesting extensions
docs.text:
What you want in the certificate goes in the extension request attribute:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extensions;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\SubjectAlternativeNameExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralNames;

$cri = $cri->withExtensionRequest(Extensions::create(
    SubjectAlternativeNameExtension::create(false, GeneralNames::create(
        DNSName::create('example.com'),
        DNSName::create('www.example.com')
    ))
));

$csr = $cri->sign(SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(), $privateKeyInfo);

withExtensionRequest() creates the attribute set if there is none and replaces any extension request already there, so calling it twice does not leave two.

Requesting is asking, not getting

A conforming issuer decides what to honour. This library's fromCSR() copies only the extensions the issuer names, and never the ones that decide what a certificate may do — basicConstraints, keyUsage, extKeyUsage, nameConstraints and the policy extensions among them. Asking for cA:TRUE gets you nothing. See Issuing from a request.

Do not mark a requested extension critical unless you know the issuer parses it: an issuer that copies a critical extension it does not recognise produces a certificate no validator will accept, so a careful one drops it instead.

docs.title: Other attributes
docs.text:
For an attribute that is not an extension request:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Attribute;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationRequest\Attributes;

$cri = $cri->withAttributes(Attributes::create(
    Attribute::fromAttributeValues($myValue)
));

withAttributes() replaces the whole set, extension request included, so set the attributes first and call withExtensionRequest() after — not the other way round.

docs.title: Changing the subject
docs.text:
$cri = $cri->withSubject(Name::fromString('cn=other.example.com'));

Immutable, like the rest: with*() returns a copy. Change it before you sign; a signed request is closed.

docs.title: Checking what you made
docs.text:
$csr->verify();                                             // true
$csr->certificationRequestInfo()->subject()->toString();
echo $csr->toPEM()->string();

And against OpenSSL, worth doing once:

openssl req -in request.csr -noout -text -verify

docs.title: Generating the key first
docs.text:
The library does not generate keys. For a request you will need one:

openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out key.pem
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out key.pem
openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out key.pem

All three write a PRIVATE KEY block, which PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM() reads directly. See Private keys.

docs.title: Issuing from a request
docs.text: This is the issuer's side, and the page with the most ways to get it wrong. Everything a certification request contains was chosen by whoever submitted it.

docs.title: The whole thing, done right
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature\SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\Extension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\ExtendedKeyUsageExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\BasicConstraintsExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Extension\KeyUsageExtension;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\TBSCertificate;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Validity;

// 1. The signature is yours to check. fromCSR() does not.
if (! $csr->verify()) {
    throw new RuntimeException('The request is not signed by the key it carries.');
}

// 2. Decide whether this subject may have this name. Nothing in the library can do that for you.
$subject = $myPolicy->nameFor($csr);

// 3. Copy only the extensions you are willing to honour, by OID.
$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, [Extension::OID_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME]);

// 4. The issuer sets everything that decides what the certificate may do.
$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate
    ->withSubject($subject)
    ->withIssuerCertificate($caCertificate)
    ->withValidity(Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 90 days'))
    ->withRandomSerialNumber()
    ->withAdditionalExtensions(
        BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false),
        KeyUsageExtension::create(true, KeyUsageExtension::DIGITAL_SIGNATURE | KeyUsageExtension::KEY_ENCIPHERMENT),
        ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::create(false, ExtendedKeyUsageExtension::OID_SERVER_AUTH)
    );

// 5. Sign with the CA's key.
$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign(
    SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(),
    $caPrivateKeyInfo
);

Each numbered step is a decision the library deliberately does not make for you.

docs.title: fromCSR() does not verify the signature
docs.text:
$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr);   // the signature was not checked

Call CertificationRequest::verify() yourself, before anything else. A request whose signature does not verify is a request whose submitter may not hold the key at all.

docs.title: What fromCSR() takes, and what it refuses
docs.text:
It takes the subject DN and the public key from the request, sets an empty issuer and an empty validity for you to fill, and adds a subjectKeyIdentifier computed from the key.

Extensions are the interesting part.

docs.title: Never copied, whatever you ask
docs.text:
These decide what a certificate is allowed to do, so they belong to the issuer. They are in TBSCertificate::FORBIDDEN_CSR_EXTENSIONS and naming one in the allow list raises InvalidArgumentException:

Extension Why basicConstraints cA:TRUE is asking to become a certificate authority keyUsage keyCertSign is the same request by another route extKeyUsage what the key may be used for nameConstraints what an intermediate may vouch for policyConstraints, policyMappings, inhibitAnyPolicy, certificatePolicies the policy processing of every validator downstream authorityKeyIdentifier names the issuer's key; the issuer sets it

docs.title: Never copied if critical and unknown
docs.text: An extension this library cannot parse, signed as critical, produces a certificate that is dead on arrival: no conforming validator accepts it, this library's own included. Such an extension is dropped even when the allow list names its OID.

docs.title: Copied only if you name it
docs.text:
$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, [Extension::OID_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME]);
$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, []);   // nothing from the request

An allow list, by OID. Anything not named is dropped.

docs.title: Leaving the argument out is deprecated
docs.text:
$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr);   // raises a deprecation notice

It copies every requested extension that is not forbidden and raises E_USER_DEPRECATED naming what it took.

That default is a deny list, and it will become an empty allow list

The set of extensions that matter grows over time, and a deny list copies every future one by default. Today a request can already carry:

  • a subjectAltName naming an identity the subject DN says nothing about — a hostname, an email address, a URI your relying parties will trust;
  • an authorityInformationAccess choosing the OCSP responder a relying party will ask.

In the next major release the default becomes the empty allow list. Pass null explicitly if you really want the current behaviour, which silences the notice and keeps the deny list:

$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, null);

Use the deprecation notice to find your call sites before the default changes.

docs.title: The subject name
docs.text:
fromCSR() copies the subject DN from the request, because that is what the structure says. It is still a name the requester chose. Whether this requester may have this name is your policy, and the library has no opinion:

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withSubject($nameYourPolicyDecided);

For a public CA this is domain validation. For an internal CA it is whatever ties a request to an identity you already authenticated. Either way it happens outside this library.

docs.title: Do not forget the validity
docs.text:
fromCSR() leaves it empty, and sign() will not fill it in. Set it:

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withValidity(Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 90 days'));

docs.title: The serial number
docs.text: sign() draws a 20-octet random one when you set none, so the safe thing is the default. See Issuing a certificate.

docs.title: A checklist
docs.text:
Before an issuance path goes anywhere near production:

  • [ ] $csr->verify() is called, and its false is handled.
  • [ ] fromCSR() is given an explicit allow list — [] if you copy nothing.
  • [ ] The subject DN is the one your policy decided, not the one the request asked for.
  • [ ] withValidity() is set.
  • [ ] basicConstraints and keyUsage are set by you, critical.
  • [ ] The serial number is random — the default, or at least nine octets.
  • [ ] The signing key is the CA's, and the algorithm matches it.
  • [ ] You have read what a request bounded by nothing can cost you: Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Three worked examples, each one complete enough to run. They assume composer require spomky-labs/pki-framework, ext-openssl and either gmp or bcmath; see Prerequisites.

  • A self-signed certificate — the shortest thing worth doing: a key, a name, a certificate, and reading it back.
  • A small certificate authority — a root, an intermediate, an end-entity certificate issued from a request, and the path that validates it.
  • Verifying a TLS chain — the one most applications actually need: a chain a peer sent, a trust store you control, and the checks validation leaves to you.

docs.title: Before you copy any of them
docs.text:
Every example omits error handling that production code needs, and says so where it matters. Two things no example can decide for you:

  • the trust anchor is yours to name — see Validating a path;
  • a successful validation is not a complete check — see What validation does not do.

The security recommendations are the short version of both.

docs.title: Generating the keys
docs.text:
The library does not generate keys. Each example starts from a PEM file written by OpenSSL:

openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out key.pem
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out ec.pem
openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out ed.pem

All three write a PRIVATE KEY block, which PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM() reads directly.

docs.title: A self-signed certificate
docs.text: The shortest complete thing: one key, one name, one certificate.

docs.title: The key
docs.text: openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out key.pem

docs.title: The script
Reading it back
Checking against OpenSSL
docs.text:
Worth doing once for any issuance path you write:

openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text
openssl verify -CAfile cert.pem cert.pem      # a self-signed certificate as its own root

docs.title: Validating it as a path
docs.text:
A self-signed certificate is a path of one, and it is its own trust anchor:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\CertificationPath;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\CertificationPath\PathValidation\PathValidationConfig;

$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($certificate, CertificateBundle::create($certificate));
$result = $path->validate(PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig());

echo $result->certificate()->tbsCertificate()->subject()->toString(), "\n";

Trusting it only proves you trust it

The anchor here is the certificate itself, which is sound only because you put it in the bundle. That is the whole point of naming the anchor: doing the same with a certificate a peer sent would prove nothing at all.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: A small certificate authority, where the issuer and the subject stop being the same party.

docs.title: A small certificate authority
docs.text: A root, an intermediate under it, and an end-entity certificate issued from a certification request — then the path that validates the result. Enough to stand up an internal PKI, and enough to show every decision an issuer makes.

docs.title: The keys
docs.text:
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out root.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out intermediate.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out server.key

docs.title: The root
The intermediate
The request, from the server's side
Issuing from the request, from the CA's side
Validating the result
Seeing the name constraint work
docs.text:
Issue a certificate for a name outside example.com from the same intermediate, and validation refuses it:

Continuing in the context of 5-validate.php, with $intermediateKey and $serverKey loaded and SubjectAlternativeNameExtension, GeneralNames and DNSName imported:

$tbs = TBSCertificate::create(
    Name::fromString('cn=www.other.test'),
    $serverKey->publicKeyInfo(),
    Name::create(),
    Validity::fromStrings('now', 'now + 90 days')
);

$tbs = $tbs->withIssuerCertificate($intermediate)->withRandomSerialNumber()
    ->withAdditionalExtensions(
        BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, false),
        // The dNSName constraint applies to THIS, not to the common name. See the note below.
        SubjectAlternativeNameExtension::create(false, GeneralNames::create(
            DNSName::create('www.other.test')
        ))
    );

$bad = $tbs->sign(SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create(), $intermediateKey);

$path = CertificationPath::create($root, $intermediate, $bad);
$path->validate($config->withTrustAnchor($root));
// PathValidationException: Name 'www.other.test' is not within the permitted subtrees.

The signature is perfectly good. The constraint is what stops it — which is the point of putting one on a delegated CA.

A dNSName constraint does not constrain the common name

Name constraints are matched by name type. A dNSName subtree is compared against the DNS names of the subjectAltName extension; the subject DN is submitted as a directoryName and is therefore compared against directoryName subtrees only. The tags have to match for a name to be constrained at all.

So the certificate above, without the subjectAltName, validates: cn=www.other.test is a directory name, no directoryName subtree exists to constrain it, and the dNSName subtree never looks at it. That is RFC 5280 behaviour, not a gap — the common name has not been an identity in the web PKI for years, which is exactly why subjectAltName is normative.

To constrain the names in a DN as well, add a directoryName subtree:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DirectoryName;

GeneralSubtrees::create(
    GeneralSubtree::create(DNSName::create('example.com')),
    GeneralSubtree::create(DirectoryName::create(Name::fromString('o=ACME Ltd, c=FR')))
);

One more reason the issuer, not the requester, sets subjectAltName: Issuing from a request.

Note the withTrustAnchor($root) here: this path was built with create(), which does not know where its first certificate came from. See Validating a path.

docs.title: What this CA does not do
docs.text: No revocation, since nothing here issues a CRL and the library has no CRL support; no serial number register, so keep your own if you intend to revoke anything; no key protection beyond the file permissions on root.key. See What validation does not do.

docs.title: Verifying a TLS chain
docs.text:
The case most applications actually have: a peer sent a chain, you hold a trust store, and you need to decide whether to believe it.

This example does the whole thing, including the parts path validation does not do.

docs.title: Getting a chain to work with
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | sed -n '/-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/,/-----END CERTIFICATE-----/p' > chain.pem

The leaf comes first, then the intermediates the server chose to send. Roots are usually not sent.

docs.title: The script
What each part is for
docs.text:
toTarget() and not fromCertificateChain(). The path is headed by a certificate from your trust store. fromCertificateChain($chain) would produce a path headed by whatever the peer put last, and would then refuse to validate without an explicit anchor — correctly, because that is not a trust decision. See Validating a path.

The peer's certificates as $intermediates. A certificate from that bundle can appear in the middle of a path, never at its head. Passing the chain there is how you let the peer help you find a path without letting them choose where it starts.

The hardened configuration. The defaults accept SHA-1 and 1024-bit RSA, for deployments that still need to. A TLS client on the public internet does not. See Configuration.

The size and count bounds. The decoder caps nesting depth; it does not cap the length of the string or the number of blocks in a bundle. See Decoding untrusted input.

The three checks after validation. Hostname, extended key usage, revocation. None of them is part of RFC 5280 section 6.1, so none of them is part of validate(). The full list is in What validation does not do.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text: This is the certificate layer, not a TLS stack. It does not speak the protocol, negotiate anything, check that the server proved possession of the key during the handshake, or implement the additional requirements TLS itself imposes on certificates. For an actual TLS connection, let the TLS implementation verify the chain; use this when you hold certificates outside a handshake — pinned material, an enrolment flow, an audit, a chain in a token.
