docs.text:
Bugs and feature requests go to the issues of the library.

A security problem is not an issue. Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion for one: doing so hands a working exploit to every user of the library before a fix exists. Report it privately, either through GitHub private vulnerability reporting or by email to security AT spomky-labs.com. The security policy says what a report should contain and what happens next.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
Pull requests go to the branch of the maintained line.

  • Follow PSR-12. make cs fixes what it can.
  • Run the test suite: make tests.
  • Write or update tests. A fix without a test that fails before it is not a fix.
  • Static analysis must pass: make st.
  • Mutation testing runs in continuous integration: make mu.
  • Rebase your branch before you open the pull request, and write commit messages that say what changed and why. You may be asked to squash.
git clone https://github.com/Spomky-Labs/pki-framework.git
cd pki-framework
composer install
make tests

CONTRIBUTING.md holds the same rules, and the code of conduct applies to every exchange.

docs.title: This documentation
docs.text:
Every documentation of Slabs lives in one repository, Spomky-Labs/docs, under projects/<project>/<version>/. These pages are in projects/pki/1.6/. The pencil at the top right of a page opens its source there.

git clone https://github.com/Spomky-Labs/docs.git
cd docs
make install                 # the toolchain, in .venv
make serve p=pki v=1.6   # http://127.0.0.1:8000, rebuilt as you save
make check                   # the strict build continuous integration runs

make check is the gate: a broken internal link, an anchor that does not exist, a page absent from the navigation or a navigation entry without a page fails the build.

One directory of that repository is one version of the library. A correction that applies to every version is made in each of them: the versions are directories, not branches.

Titles are in sentence case; names keep their capitals. Every code block is expected to run against the version the page documents.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The library is distributed on Packagist; the source lives on GitHub.

composer require spomky-labs/pki-framework

There is no bundle, no configuration file and no service to register. Every class is constructed through a static factory — create(), fromPEM(), fromDER(), fromASN1() — and nothing is read from the environment.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\Certificate;

require 'vendor/autoload.php';

$certificate = Certificate::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('server.crt'));

Everything lives under the SpomkyLabs\Pki namespace, autoloaded with PSR-4 from src/.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
A release line is named 1.x, maintained on a branch named 1.x.x. Only the latest stable line receives fixes, security fixes included, and nothing is backported to an older one: upgrade before you report a problem. The lines currently maintained are listed in SECURITY.md.

This documentation is published once per maintained line. The version selector in the header of the site switches between them, and the root of the site leads to the newest one.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion for a security problem. Report it privately, either through GitHub private vulnerability reporting or by email to security AT spomky-labs.com. What a report should contain, and what happens next, are in the security policy.

docs.title: PHP and required extensions
docs.text:
• PHP 8.1 or later.
  • mbstring, required. The X.520 string preparation steps that make name comparison work transcode and normalise text with it.

docs.title: Arithmetic: gmp or bcmath
docs.text:
Serial numbers, RSA moduli and large integers do not fit in a PHP integer, so they go through brick/math, which is installed with the library. It uses gmp if it is loaded, bcmath if it is not, and falls back to a pure-PHP implementation otherwise.

Install gmp, or bcmath. The fallback is correct but slow enough to matter as soon as you parse certificates in a loop or validate a path.

docs.title: openssl: needed to sign and to verify
docs.text:
Signing and verifying go through a crypto engine, and the only one shipped is OpenSSLCrypto. Without ext-openssl, Crypto::getDefault() throws, and with it every call that signs or verifies:

  • TBSCertificate::sign(), CertificationRequestInfo::sign(), AttributeCertificateInfo::sign();
  • Certificate::verify(), CertificationRequest::verify(), AttributeCertificate::verify();
  • CertificationPath::validate() and ACValidator::validate().

Reading, writing and inspecting structures need none of it. A service that only parses certificates it is handed runs without openssl.

docs.title: sodium: Ed25519 where OpenSSL has no EdDSA
docs.text:
Ed25519 and Ed448 are in the default set of allowed signature algorithms, but whether a signature made with them can actually be checked depends on the runtime. The OpenSSL extension only grew EdDSA recently; ext-sodium, bundled since PHP 7.2, covers Ed25519 alone.

Verification fails closed where the runtime cannot do it, which surfaces as a path that does not validate. Ask before you configure rather than after:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto\OpenSSLCrypto;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Asymmetric\Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier;

$crypto = new OpenSSLCrypto();

if (! $crypto->supportsSignatureAlgorithm(Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier::create())) {
    // narrow the configured set rather than have a chain refused during validation
}

See Configuration.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Extension Status Without it mbstring Required The library does not install gmp or bcmath Strongly recommended Correct, but slow on large integers openssl Needed to sign or verify Parsing works; signing, verifying and path validation throw sodium Optional Ed25519 cannot be verified on a runtime whose OpenSSL has no EdDSA

docs.title: Provided features
docs.text: PKI Framework is a set of data structures and one validator. Each namespace of the library maps to a specification, and the pages of this documentation follow the same split.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text: Namespace What lives there SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1 ASN.1 types and the DER codec: ASN.1 and DER SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding PEM, a single block or a bundle: Textual encoding (PEM) SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes Keys, algorithm identifiers, signatures: Keys, algorithms and signatures SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge The engine that signs and verifies: The crypto engine SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501 Distinguished names, attributes, comparison: Names and attributes SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509 Certificates, requests, attribute certificates, paths

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text:
ASN.1, after X.690. Every universal type, primitive and constructed, with DER encoding and decoding. Implicit and explicit tagging, application and private classes, indefinite length, constructed strings. A decoded element is handed back through UnspecifiedType, which makes you say what you expected.

X.509 certificates, after RFC 5280. Reading, building and signing, with twenty-odd extensions parsed into their own classes: basic constraints, key usage, extended key usage, subject and issuer alternative names, name constraints, policy constraints, policy mappings, inhibit anyPolicy, certificate policies, authority and subject key identifiers, CRL distribution points, freshest CRL, authority and subject information access, subject directory attributes, target information, AA controls, and no revocation available. An extension the library does not know becomes an UnknownExtension rather than an error.

Certification path building and validation, after RFC 5280 section 6. All paths or the shortest path from a trust list to a target, then the full validation algorithm: signatures, validity periods, basic constraints and path length, key usage, name constraints, and the policy tree with mapping, explicit policy and anyPolicy inhibition.

Certification requests, after RFC 2986. PKCS #10: reading, building, signing, verifying, and the extension request attribute. Turning one into a certificate is the issuer's job and is deliberately narrow.

Attribute certificates, after RFC 5755. Holder, issuer, validity period, the IETF attribute syntax and the role, group, access identity, charging identity and authentication info attributes. Validation of the holder and issuer paths, the targets, and the attribute authority.

Keys, after PKCS and RFC 8410. RSA, EC, RSASSA-PSS, Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448, as PKCS #8 OneAsymmetricKey / PrivateKeyInfo, as SubjectPublicKeyInfo, and in their own legacy formats.

Names, after X.501 and X.520. Distinguished names from and to the RFC 4514 string form, the standard attribute types, and name comparison with the matching rules and string preparation the specifications ask for.

docs.title: What is not implemented
docs.text:
These are design decisions, not gaps waiting for a patch.

No network. The library never opens a connection. Nothing is fetched from an authority information access extension, a CRL distribution point or an OCSP responder.

No revocation checking. There is no CRL parser and no OCSP client. A revoked certificate validates: see What validation does not do.

No system trust store. Trust anchors are an input to validation, never a discovery.

No RSASSA-PSS signatures. A PSS-signed certificate is refused when it is parsed. The OID is deliberately absent from the default set of allowed signature algorithms, since allowing it would advertise a capability that does not exist.

No hostname matching. Checking that a certificate is the right one for example.com is a step of its own, which the library does not perform. It gives you the subject DN and the subject alternative names; the comparison, and the rules of the protocol you are speaking, are yours.

No key generation. Generate keys with ext-openssl, ext-sodium or anything else, then read them in with PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM().

docs.title: Security recommendations
docs.text:
The library parses, builds and validates structures. It does not decide what you trust. This page lists every decision it hands back to you, and every default that is looser than a new deployment would choose.

Read it before you ship. Each item links to the page that explains it in full.

docs.title: Name the trust anchor
docs.text:
A path validated without an anchor proves nothing

Left to itself, validation falls back to the first certificate of the path — one the peer chose — and confirms only that the chain is internally consistent.

Build the path from the certificates you trust and let the library find its way to the target:

$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($leafFromPeer, $trustAnchors, $intermediatesFromPeer);
$result = $path->validate(PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig());

A path built by fromCertificateChain() refuses to validate without an explicit anchor. One built by create() raises a deprecation notice when it falls back, so you can find the call sites before the fallback is removed in the next major release. See Validating a path.

docs.title: Treat a certification request as untrusted input
docs.text:
fromCSR() does not verify the signature, and the default extension policy is a deny list

Call CertificationRequest::verify() yourself, then name the extensions you are willing to honour:

$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, [Extension::OID_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME]);

Leaving the second argument out copies every requested extension that is not forbidden and raises a deprecation notice. That default is a deny list, so every extension invented in the future would be copied by it. See Issuing from a request.

docs.title: Check revocation yourself
docs.text: Path validation says the chain is well-formed and leads to an anchor you named. It does not say the certificate is still valid. The library has no CRL parser and no OCSP client, and never opens a connection, so a revoked certificate validates. See What validation does not do.

docs.title: Narrow the signature algorithms and the RSA floor
docs.text:
The defaults carry what deployed PKIs still use, not what a new one should accept.

Setting Default Hardened Signature algorithms DEFAULT_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS, which includes SHA-1 HARDENED_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS RSA modulus DEFAULT_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE, 1024 bits HARDENED_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE, 2048 bits 
$config = PathValidationConfig::defaultConfig()
    ->withAllowedSignatureAlgorithms(...PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_ALLOWED_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS)
    ->withMinimumRSAKeySize(PathValidationConfig::HARDENED_MINIMUM_RSA_KEY_SIZE);

Chosen-prefix collisions against SHA-1 have been practical since 2020, and the CA/Browser Forum has required 2048-bit RSA since 2014. The defaults are what they are because raising them in a patch release would silently cut off legacy enterprise and device PKIs. If yours is not one of them, harden it. These are the values the defaults will become in a future major release. See Configuration.

docs.title: Know whether your runtime can verify EdDSA
docs.text: Ed25519 and Ed448 are allowed by default, but verification depends on the extensions loaded: the OpenSSL extension only grew EdDSA recently, and ext-sodium covers Ed25519 alone. Verification fails closed, which surfaces as a chain that will not validate. Ask up front with OpenSSLCrypto::supportsSignatureAlgorithm() rather than debugging it later. See Prerequisites.

docs.title: Name the attribute authorities you trust
docs.text: Attribute certificate validation does not implement RFC 5755 section 5 check 4 on its own. Without ACValidationConfig::withTrustedAttributeAuthorities(), the validator accepts whatever end-entity certificate the issuer path ends in. See Validating an attribute certificate.

docs.title: Compare certificates with the right question
docs.text:
• Certificate::equals() compares the two encodings octet by octet. CertificateBundle::contains() is built on it.
  • Certificate::hasEqualSubjectIdentity() asks the looser question: same subject, same key, same serial number. It is not an identity check — two certificates can agree on all three and still be issued by different issuers with different extensions.

docs.title: Bound what you decode
docs.text:
DER decoding recurses, so nesting is capped at Element::DEFAULT_MAX_NESTING_DEPTH, 64 levels. A real X.509 structure rarely nests deeper than ten. If you decode material from the open internet, lower it:

Element::setMaxNestingDepth(16);

The cap is global process state, not per call. Size is yours to bound: the library decodes the string you give it, so cap the length of an upload before you hand it over. See Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: Give certificates a random serial number
docs.text:
A constant serial number removes the unpredictability that protects issuance against collision attacks, and breaks CRL revocation, which identifies a certificate by the (issuer, serial number) pair. sign() draws one when none was set. If you set one yourself, draw at least nine octets — MIN_RANDOM_SERIAL_SIZE — which is the 64 bits of CSPRNG output the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements ask for, plus the octet the sign bit costs:

$tbsCertificate = $tbsCertificate->withRandomSerialNumber(); // 20 octets, the RFC 5280 maximum

See Issuing a certificate.

docs.title: Leave version 1 and version 2 intermediates alone
docs.text: RFC 5280 section 6.1.4 (k) lets a version 1 or version 2 certificate act as a CA only once the application has confirmed out of band that it is one. withLegacyV1IntermediatesTrusted(true) is how you state that you did. Do not set it to work around a chain you do not understand.

docs.title: Declare the critical extensions you handle
docs.text: A critical extension the validator does not recognise makes validation fail, as it should. If your application processes one by its own means, say so with withAdditionalCriticalExtensions(). Naming an extension there means you check it — the validator then only stops objecting.

docs.title: Hostname matching is yours
docs.text: The library gives you the subject DN and the subject alternative names. It does not check that a certificate is the right one for example.com, and path validation never looks at a hostname. That comparison, with the rules of the protocol you are speaking, is a step of your own.

docs.title: Keys, algorithms and signatures
docs.text:
SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes holds three things that travel together: a key, an algorithm identifier that says what kind of key it is and what may be done with it, and a signature.

The library does not generate keys. Generate them with ext-openssl, ext-sodium or a command line, and read the result in.

docs.title: Two levels of key
docs.text:
The container. PrivateKeyInfo (a PKCS #8 OneAsymmetricKey) and PublicKeyInfo (a SubjectPublicKeyInfo) are the wrappers that carry an algorithm identifier beside the key material. This is what the rest of the library takes and returns: a certificate holds a PublicKeyInfo, and sign() takes a PrivateKeyInfo.

The key itself. RSAPrivateKey, ECPublicKey, Ed25519PrivateKey and their siblings are the algorithm-specific structures inside. Go down to them when you need a modulus, a curve name or the raw point.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PrivateKeyInfo;

$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('key.pem'));

$publicKeyInfo = $privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo();   // derived, or read from the container
$rsa = $privateKeyInfo->privateKey();                // RSAPrivateKey, ECPrivateKey, Ed25519PrivateKey, …

Going up is as short:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PublicKeyInfo;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\RSA\RSAPublicKey;

$publicKeyInfo = PublicKeyInfo::fromPublicKey(RSAPublicKey::fromPEM($pem));

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
Algorithm Private key class Public key class RSA RSA\RSAPrivateKey RSA\RSAPublicKey RSASSA-PSS RSA\RSASSAPSSPrivateKey — Elliptic curve EC\ECPrivateKey EC\ECPublicKey Ed25519 RFC8410\Curve25519\Ed25519PrivateKey RFC8410\Curve25519\Ed25519PublicKey Ed448 RFC8410\Curve448\Ed448PrivateKey RFC8410\Curve448\Ed448PublicKey X25519 RFC8410\Curve25519\X25519PrivateKey RFC8410\Curve25519\X25519PublicKey X448 RFC8410\Curve448\X448PrivateKey RFC8410\Curve448\X448PublicKey

X25519 and X448 are key agreement keys, not signing keys: the library reads and writes them, and nothing signs with them.

RSASSA-PSS keys are read, but PSS signatures are not implemented. A PSS-signed certificate is refused when it is parsed, and the OID is deliberately absent from the default set of allowed signature algorithms.

docs.title: Key identifiers
docs.text:
RFC 5280 gives two ways to name a key, and PublicKeyInfo implements both:

$publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier();     // method 1: the SHA-1 of the public key bit string, 20 bytes
$publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier64();   // method 2: 8 bytes, the type-and-value form

Method 1 is what goes into a subjectKeyIdentifier extension and what an authorityKeyIdentifier points at. TBSCertificate::withIssuerCertificate() and fromCSR() set them for you.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Private keys — reading them, the formats, what each one gives you.
  • Public keys — the same from the other side, and getting one out of a certificate.
  • Algorithm identifiers — the OIDs, the classes, and the factory.
  • Signatures — the Signature types and their encodings.
  • The crypto engine — who actually signs and verifies, and what the runtime can do.

docs.title: Algorithm identifiers
docs.text:
An AlgorithmIdentifier is an OID and, sometimes, parameters. It appears everywhere: beside a key to say what kind of key it is, beside a signature to say how it was made, inside an extension to name a digest.

Every one is its own class, so a signature algorithm is a type rather than a string you have to recognise.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature\SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier;

$algorithm = SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier::create();

$algorithm->oid();    // "1.2.840.113549.1.1.11"
$algorithm->name();   // a human-readable name, for an error message

docs.title: The families
docs.text:
The interfaces under AlgorithmIdentifier\Feature are what a signature takes when any member of a family will do.

Interface Means SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier may sign a certificate, a request or an attribute certificate HashAlgorithmIdentifier a digest CipherAlgorithmIdentifier a symmetric cipher BlockCipherAlgorithmIdentifier a block cipher, with a block size and an IV AsymmetricCryptoAlgorithmIdentifier names a key type PRFAlgorithmIdentifier a pseudo-random function EncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier encrypts

TBSCertificate::sign() takes a SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier, so passing a hash is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

docs.title: Signature algorithms
docs.text:
Class, under AlgorithmIdentifier\Signature Accepted by default in path validation SHA1WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier yes SHA224WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier yes SHA256WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier yes SHA384WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier yes SHA512WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier yes ECDSAWithSHA1AlgorithmIdentifier yes ECDSAWithSHA224AlgorithmIdentifier yes ECDSAWithSHA256AlgorithmIdentifier yes ECDSAWithSHA384AlgorithmIdentifier yes ECDSAWithSHA512AlgorithmIdentifier yes MD2WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier no MD4WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier no MD5WithRSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier no

Ed25519 and Ed448 sign too, through Asymmetric\Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier and Asymmetric\Ed448AlgorithmIdentifier: in RFC 8410 the key type and the signature algorithm are the same OID. Both are accepted by default, subject to what the runtime can do.

The MD2, MD4 and MD5 classes exist so that a certificate signed with one can be parsed and reported. They are left out of the default accepted set: chosen-prefix collisions against MD5 have been practical since 2009, which is enough to forge a certificate that verifies, and no authority in service still signs with them.

RSASSA-PSS is not implemented. Asymmetric\RSAPSSSSAEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier models the identifier, and a PSS-signed certificate is refused when it is parsed. The OID is deliberately absent from the default accepted set: allowing it would advertise a capability that does not exist. Implementing it will mean binding the parameters as well as the OID, since Certificate::fromASN1() compares only the OIDs of the outer and signed algorithm identifiers, which would otherwise leave a hash, MGF and salt length downgrade open.

docs.title: Key algorithms
Hashes and ciphers
docs.text:
Under AlgorithmIdentifier\Hash: MD5, SHA1, SHA224, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512, and the RFC 4231 HMAC identifiers HMACWithSHA1 through HMACWithSHA512.

Under AlgorithmIdentifier\Cipher: DESCBC, DESEDE3CBC, RC2CBC, AES128CBC, AES192CBC, AES256CBC. A block cipher identifier carries its initialisation vector, which is why Crypto::encrypt() takes no separate IV.

docs.title: Reading one you were handed
docs.text:
AlgorithmIdentifier::fromASN1() dispatches on the OID and returns the right class:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\AlgorithmIdentifier;

$algorithm = AlgorithmIdentifier::fromASN1($sequence);

An OID the library does not know comes back as a GenericAlgorithmIdentifier, which keeps the OID and the parameters as they were. Nothing is lost and nothing throws: you can inspect and re-encode an identifier the library has no class for.

docs.title: Adding your own
docs.text:
Implement AlgorithmIdentifierProvider — supportsOID(string $oid): bool and getClassByOID(string $oid): string — and hand it to the factory:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\AlgorithmIdentifierFactory;

$factory = AlgorithmIdentifierFactory::create($myProvider);

$factory->getClass('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1');   // your class name, or null
$algorithm = $factory->parse($sequence);     // your class, or one of the library's

Your class extends SpecificAlgorithmIdentifier and implements the Feature interface of its family — SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier for a signature algorithm, which is what makes it acceptable to sign().

A provider adds, it does not override

The built-in map is consulted first, so a provider cannot replace an identifier the library already ships. AlgorithmIdentifier::fromASN1() uses a factory with no providers at all, so an OID only your provider knows comes back from it as a GenericAlgorithmIdentifier. Call your own factory's parse() where you want your classes.

Signing with it is a separate matter: the crypto engine has to know how, and the one shipped speaks the algorithms OpenSSL does.

docs.title: Private keys
docs.text: PrivateKeyInfo is the PKCS #8 container — an OneAsymmetricKey, after RFC 5958 — and the type every sign() in the library takes.

docs.title: Reading one
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PrivateKeyInfo;

$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromPEM(PEM::fromFile('key.pem'));
$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromDER($der);

fromPEM() accepts three labels and normalises the two legacy ones into the container:

PEM label What it holds Read as PRIVATE KEY PKCS #8, the modern format decoded directly RSA PRIVATE KEY PKCS #1, what openssl genrsa used to write wrapped EC PRIVATE KEY SEC 1, what openssl ecparam -genkey writes wrapped

Any other label — ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY among them — throws UnexpectedValueException. The library has no password-based key derivation; see Textual encoding (PEM).

To generate one to read:

openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out key.pem   # PRIVATE KEY
openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out ed.pem                              # PRIVATE KEY

docs.title: What the container gives you
docs.text:
$privateKeyInfo->algorithmIdentifier();   // what kind of key this is
$privateKeyInfo->privateKeyData();        // the inner structure, still encoded
$privateKeyInfo->privateKey();            // the inner structure, decoded
$privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo();         // the matching PublicKeyInfo
$privateKeyInfo->version();
$privateKeyInfo->toPEM()->string();

publicKeyInfo() returns the public key carried in the container when there is one, and derives it from the private key otherwise. It is how you get the PublicKeyInfo a certificate or a certification request needs:

$tbsCertificate = TBSCertificate::create(
    $subject,
    $privateKeyInfo->publicKeyInfo(),   // here
    $issuer,
    $validity
);

docs.title: The key inside
docs.text:
privateKey() returns the algorithm-specific structure, decoded from privateKeyData():

RSAElliptic curveEd25519 and Ed448 
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\RSA\RSAPrivateKey;

/** @var RSAPrivateKey $key */
$key = $privateKeyInfo->privateKey();

$key->modulus();          // decimal string: it does not fit in an int
$key->publicExponent();
$key->privateExponent();
$key->prime1();
$key->prime2();
$key->exponent1();
$key->exponent2();
$key->coefficient();

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\EC\ECPrivateKey;

/** @var ECPrivateKey $key */
$key = $privateKeyInfo->privateKey();

$key->hasNamedCurve();
$key->namedCurve();          // the OID of the curve
$key->privateKeyOctets();
$key->publicKey();           // ECPublicKey, when the structure carries it

OpenSSL strips the curve, RFC 5915 requires it

OpenSSL drops the named curve from the inner ECPrivateKey when it wraps it into a PrivateKeyInfo, although RFC 5915 says the parameters must always be there. The library puts it back from the algorithm identifier of the container, so namedCurve() answers either way.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\RFC8410\Curve25519\Ed25519PrivateKey;

/** @var Ed25519PrivateKey $key */
$key = $privateKeyInfo->privateKey();

$key->privateKeyData();
$key->publicKey();

RFC 8410 encodes the key as an OCTET STRING inside the privateKey OCTET STRING, so the material is doubly wrapped. The library unwraps both.

An algorithm the library does not know raises RuntimeException from privateKey(), with the algorithm name in the message. The container itself still decoded, so algorithmIdentifier() and privateKeyData() work: you can inspect what you were handed before giving up on it.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Asymmetric\PrivateKeyInfo;

$privateKeyInfo = PrivateKeyInfo::fromPrivateKey($rsaPrivateKey);

file_put_contents('key.pem', $privateKeyInfo->toPEM()->string());
echo $privateKeyInfo->toDER();

Each key class also writes its own legacy format, if that is what you need:

$rsaPrivateKey->toPEM()->string();   // -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
$ecPrivateKey->toPEM()->string();    // -----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY-----

A private key in a variable is a private key on a core dump

The library holds key material as PHP strings and makes no attempt to wipe them: PHP gives no way to. Read keys from a path only your process can read, do not log the objects — var_dump($privateKeyInfo) prints the key — and prefer passing the PrivateKeyInfo around to re-reading the file.

docs.title: Public keys
docs.text: PublicKeyInfo is the SubjectPublicKeyInfo of RFC 5280: an algorithm identifier and a bit string. It is what a certificate carries and what every verify() in the library takes.

docs.title: Where one comes from
What it gives you
docs.text:
$publicKeyInfo->algorithmIdentifier();   // RSA, EC, Ed25519, …
$publicKeyInfo->publicKeyData();         // the BitString, as encoded
$publicKeyInfo->publicKey();             // the decoded key
$publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier();         // 20 bytes, RFC 5280 method 1
$publicKeyInfo->keyIdentifier64();       // 8 bytes, method 2
$publicKeyInfo->toPEM()->string();

docs.title: The key inside
Verifying with one
docs.text:
Verification takes the PublicKeyInfo, not the inner key:

$certificate->verify($issuerCertificate->tbsCertificate()->subjectPublicKeyInfo());

See The crypto engine.

verify() is not validation

Certificate::verify() answers one question: was this certificate signed by the key you passed? It says nothing about whether that key belongs to anyone you trust, whether the certificate is in date, or whether its issuer was allowed to sign it. Those are path validation.

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text: A signature is not just bytes: ECDSA writes a SEQUENCE of two integers, RSA writes an octet string, and EdDSA writes a fixed-length string. Signature is the type that keeps the difference straight.

docs.title: The classes
docs.text: Class, under CryptoTypes\Signature Encoding RSASignature the signature value as it is ECSignature a SEQUENCE of r and s Ed25519Signature 64 bytes Ed448Signature 114 bytes GenericSignature a bit string and the algorithm that made it

docs.title: Where one comes from
docs.text:
Reading a structure:

$signature = $certificate->signatureValue();
$signature = $csr->signature();
$signature = $attributeCertificate->signatureValue();

Signing:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto;

$signature = Crypto::getDefault()->sign($data, $privateKeyInfo, $algorithm);

You rarely call that directly — TBSCertificate::sign() and its siblings do it for you and hand back the signed structure. See Issuing a certificate.

From raw bytes, when the algorithm says how to read them:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Signature\Signature;

$signature = Signature::fromSignatureData($bytes, $algorithm);

That is the factory the engine uses: it dispatches on the algorithm and builds the right class, so an ECDSA signature is parsed into r and s rather than kept as an opaque blob.

docs.title: Reading one
docs.text:
$signature->bitString()->string();   // the bytes, whatever the class

ECSignature exposes the two halves, which is what you need when bridging to a library that wants them separately:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\Signature\ECSignature;

/** @var ECSignature $signature */
$signature->r();         // decimal string
$signature->s();
$signature->toDER();     // the SEQUENCE

ECSignature::create($r, $s) builds one from the two integers, and fromDER() reads the SEQUENCE back.

r and s are decimal strings, not integers

They are coordinates on a curve: on P-521 they do not fit in a PHP integer. Pass them to brick/math if you need arithmetic, and to EC\ECConversion::numberToOctets() if you need the fixed-length octet form that JWS and COSE use.

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
Verification takes the data, the signature, the public key and the algorithm:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto;

$valid = Crypto::getDefault()->verify($data, $signature, $publicKeyInfo, $algorithm);

Again, the structures do it for you:

$certificate->verify($issuerPublicKeyInfo);
$csr->verify();                                  // self-signed by definition
$attributeCertificate->verify($issuerPublicKeyInfo);

Each one re-encodes the signed part, hands it to the engine with the algorithm the structure names, and returns a boolean.

A true from verify() is one fact, not trust

It says the signature was made by the key you passed. It does not say the key belongs to anyone, that the certificate is in date, or that its issuer was allowed to sign it. Those are path validation.

docs.title: Mismatched algorithm and key
docs.text:
The engine checks that the signature algorithm and the key agree before it does anything: an ECDSA algorithm with an RSA key raises UnexpectedValueException rather than failing somewhere inside OpenSSL.

An algorithm the runtime cannot handle fails the same way, with the algorithm named in the message. See The crypto engine.

docs.title: The crypto engine
docs.text:
Every structure in the library is data. The arithmetic — signing, verifying, encrypting — happens in a Crypto engine, and the one shipped wraps ext-openssl.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto;

$crypto = Crypto::getDefault();

getDefault() returns an OpenSSLCrypto when OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER is defined, and throws RuntimeException otherwise. Nothing is cached: it is a new instance each call, and the engine holds no state worth keeping.

Every method that needs an engine takes one as an optional last argument and falls back to the default:

$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign($algorithm, $privateKeyInfo);           // the default engine
$certificate = $tbsCertificate->sign($algorithm, $privateKeyInfo, $crypto);  // yours

$path->validate($config);           // the default engine
$path->validate($config, $crypto);  // yours

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
$signature = $crypto->sign($data, $privateKeyInfo, $signatureAlgorithm);
$valid = $crypto->verify($data, $signature, $publicKeyInfo, $signatureAlgorithm);

$ciphertext = $crypto->encrypt($plaintext, $key, $cipherAlgorithm);
$plaintext = $crypto->decrypt($ciphertext, $key, $cipherAlgorithm);

encrypt() and decrypt() are there for the PKCS structures that need a block cipher. Padding is yours: the engine encrypts with zero padding and raw data, and the initialisation vector comes from the algorithm identifier, which is why there is no separate IV argument. They are not a general-purpose encryption API — reach for sodium for that.

docs.title: The algorithm and the key must agree
docs.text:
Before anything else, sign() and verify() check that the signature algorithm accepts the key type. An ECDSA algorithm with an RSA key raises UnexpectedValueException naming both, rather than failing somewhere inside OpenSSL with a message about a PEM header.

A cipher whose key is the wrong length is refused the same way, with the expected size in the message.

docs.title: What this runtime can do
docs.text:
RSA and ECDSA with SHA-1 through SHA-512 work wherever ext-openssl does. EdDSA is the one that depends on the runtime.

  • PHP 8.5 verifies Ed25519 and Ed448 through openssl_verify().
  • Older runtimes have no EdDSA in the OpenSSL extension at all. Ed25519 then goes through ext-sodium, bundled since PHP 7.2. There is no equivalent for Ed448.
  • Signing needs OpenSSL either way: ext-sodium could sign Ed25519, but it cannot produce an Ed448 signature, and the engine does not grow a second signing path for the half case. Signing with an EdDSA algorithm the OpenSSL extension does not support raises UnexpectedValueException.

The engine works out what OpenSSL can do by verifying RFC 8032's known-good test vector for each curve, once per process and once per curve — an extension without EdDSA reports the vector as invalid rather than raising, which is exactly the failure this guards against. Ask before you configure:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto\OpenSSLCrypto;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Asymmetric\Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\AlgorithmIdentifier\Asymmetric\Ed448AlgorithmIdentifier;

$crypto = new OpenSSLCrypto();

$crypto->supportsSignatureAlgorithm(Ed25519AlgorithmIdentifier::create());   // OpenSSL or sodium
$crypto->supportsSignatureAlgorithm(Ed448AlgorithmIdentifier::create());     // OpenSSL only

Verification fails closed, which looks like a bad chain

Ed25519 and Ed448 are in the default set of allowed signature algorithms, so a chain signed with one reaches the engine and is then refused on a runtime that cannot check it. From the outside that is indistinguishable from an invalid signature. If your deployment may meet EdDSA, probe for it at boot and either narrow the allowed set or say plainly that the runtime is missing an extension.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Thrown When RuntimeException no OpenSSL at all (getDefault()), or an OpenSSL call failed; the message carries OpenSSL's own UnexpectedValueException the algorithm and the key disagree, the cipher key is the wrong length, or the runtime cannot do EdDSA

verify() returns false for a signature that simply does not match. It throws only when the question could not be asked.

docs.title: Replacing it
docs.text:
Crypto is an abstract class with four methods. Extend it to put signing behind a hardware module, a remote service or a key management system:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\Crypto;

final class HsmCrypto extends Crypto
{
    public function sign(string $data, PrivateKeyInfo $privkey_info, SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier $algo): Signature
    {
        // ask the module, then:
        return Signature::fromSignatureData($bytes, $algo);
    }

    // verify(), encrypt(), decrypt()
}

Pass it as the last argument everywhere, or make it the one your application resolves — the library never reads a global, so there is nothing to register.

sign() receives the private key as a value

The signature of Crypto::sign() takes a PrivateKeyInfo, so an engine that never sees key material needs a PrivateKeyInfo that stands for a key it holds elsewhere — a handle rather than a secret. OpenSSLCrypto writes it out as PEM and hands it to openssl_sign(); yours is free to read only the algorithm identifier and the key identifier, and look the real key up.

docs.title: Migrating from the sop libraries
docs.text:
PKI Framework started as a fork of the libraries published at github.com/sop by Joni Eskelinen — sop/asn1, sop/x509, sop/x501, sop/crypto-types, sop/crypto-encoding, sop/crypto-bridge. It has diverged substantially since, and the two are no longer interchangeable. All credit for the original work goes to its developer.

This page is for code that used the originals.

docs.title: One package instead of six
docs.text:
composer remove sop/asn1 sop/x509 sop/x501 sop/crypto-types sop/crypto-encoding sop/crypto-bridge
composer require spomky-labs/pki-framework

Everything is in one package now, autoloaded under one namespace.

docs.title: The namespace
docs.text:
Was Is Sop\ASN1\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\… Sop\X509\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\… Sop\X501\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\… Sop\CryptoTypes\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoTypes\… Sop\CryptoEncoding\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\… Sop\CryptoBridge\… SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoBridge\…

The class names and the directory layout under each are unchanged, so a search and replace over your use statements covers most of the work:

grep -rl 'Sop\\' src tests | xargs sed -i \
  -e 's/Sop\\ASN1\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\ASN1\\/g' \
  -e 's/Sop\\X509\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\X509\\/g' \
  -e 's/Sop\\X501\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\X501\\/g' \
  -e 's/Sop\\CryptoTypes\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\CryptoTypes\\/g' \
  -e 's/Sop\\CryptoEncoding\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\CryptoEncoding\\/g' \
  -e 's/Sop\\CryptoBridge\\/SpomkyLabs\\Pki\\CryptoBridge\\/g'

Check the diff: a string mentioning Sop\ in a message or a fixture is not a class reference.

docs.title: new becomes create()
docs.text:
This is the change that touches the most lines. Constructors are private or protected, so every class is built through a static factory and new no longer compiles.

// was
$seq = new Sequence(new Integer(1), new UTF8String('x'));
$name = new Name(...$rdns);
$validity = new Validity($notBefore, $notAfter);
$ext = new BasicConstraintsExtension(true, true, 1);

// is
$seq = Sequence::create(Integer::create(1), UTF8String::create('x'));
$name = Name::create(...$rdns);
$validity = Validity::create($notBefore, $notAfter);
$ext = BasicConstraintsExtension::create(true, true, 1);

The rule is mechanical: new X(…) becomes X::create(…), with the same arguments. The named factories you already used — fromPEM(), fromDER(), fromASN1(), fromString() — are unchanged.

new OpenSSLCrypto() still works, since the crypto engine is meant to be extended. Step 2 of the order below is the cheap way to find the rest: a missed new is a hard failure, not a silent one.

docs.title: Immutability
docs.text:
Objects do not change. Every with*() returns a copy, and the original is untouched:

$tbs->withRandomSerialNumber();              // discarded
$tbs = $tbs->withRandomSerialNumber();       // what you meant

That was true of the originals in most places and is now true everywhere, including Extensions, AttributeCollection and the ASN.1 structures.

docs.title: DateTimeImmutable
docs.text:
Dates are DateTimeImmutable, never DateTime:

$validity->notBefore()->dateTime();          // DateTimeImmutable
PathValidationConfig::create(new DateTimeImmutable(), 3);

docs.title: Large integers
docs.text:
Serial numbers, RSA moduli and ASN.1 integers come back as decimal strings, with brick/math underneath:

$tbs->serialNumber();                        // "2569673129085639595562975411803018896"
$integer->number();                          // decimal string
$integer->intNumber();                       // int, throws if it does not fit
$integer->getValue();                        // BigInteger

Comparing serial numbers as PHP integers silently stops working above PHP_INT_MAX. Compare the strings, or use BigInteger.

docs.title: Behaviour that changed, and will break code
docs.text: These are the ones a search and replace will not find. Each is deliberate.

docs.title: Path validation needs a trust anchor
docs.text:
// was: validated against the path's own first certificate, silently
$path->validate($config);

// is
$path->validate($config->withTrustAnchor($root));
// or, better, build the path from your trust list
$path = CertificationPath::toTarget($target, $trustAnchors, $intermediates);
$path->validate($config);

A path from fromCertificateChain() now throws without an anchor. A path from create() raises a deprecation notice and still falls back, so you can find your call sites before the fallback goes. See Validating a path.

docs.title: fromCSR() no longer copies every requested extension
docs.text:
// was: every requested extension was copied
$tbs = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr);

// is: name what you honour
$tbs = TBSCertificate::fromCSR($csr, [Extension::OID_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME]);

The extensions that decide what a certificate may do are never copied, whatever you pass. Leaving the argument out raises a deprecation notice and will become an empty allow list. See Issuing from a request.

docs.title: Certificate::equals() is now an exact comparison
docs.text:
It compares the two encodings octet by octet. It used to compare the serial number, the subject key identifier and the subject DN — three public values anyone can repeat — so it reported two certificates as the same when they differed in issuer, validity, every extension and the signature.

CertificateBundle::contains() is built on it and became exact with it. If you relied on the looser grouping, hasEqualSubjectIdentity() is it — and read what it does not tell you.

docs.title: Signature algorithms and key sizes are filtered
docs.text: Path validation refuses an algorithm outside allowedSignatureAlgorithms() and an RSA modulus below minimumRSAKeySize(). MD2, MD4 and MD5 are refused by default; the defaults still accept SHA-1 and 1024 bits. A chain that used to validate may now be refused — which is the point. See Configuration.

docs.title: RSASSA-PSS certificates are refused when parsed
docs.text: Not implemented, and deliberately absent from the allowed set rather than advertised and broken.

docs.title: Decoding is bounded and its exceptions are normalised
docs.text: Nesting is capped at 64 levels, and nothing but DecodeException escapes Element::fromDER() — the original type is kept as its previous. A catch for something narrower may stop matching. See Decoding untrusted input.

docs.title: Serial numbers are random by default
docs.text: sign() draws a 20-octet serial number when none was set, rather than writing a zero. A fixed serial number below nine octets raises a deprecation notice.

docs.title: Repeated optional fields are refused
docs.text: A structure carrying the same context-specific tag twice raises DecodeException rather than being read as its last copy.

docs.title: Name comparison prepares each side under its own syntax
docs.text: The same name written as a BMPString and as a PrintableString now compares equal, where it used to be two different names — which meant a directoryName a constraint excluded was reachable by re-encoding it. See Comparing names.

docs.title: PHP version
docs.text: PHP 8.1 or later, and mbstring is required. See Prerequisites.

docs.title: A migration order that works
docs.text:
1. Replace the packages, run the namespace replacement, and let the autoloader find what is left.
  2. Replace new X(…) with X::create(…), guided by the errors. Private constructors make every missed one a hard failure rather than a silent one.
  3. Run your test suite with E_USER_DEPRECATED visible. The two notices that matter — the path validation fallback and the fromCSR() deny list — are both security decisions, and both are going away.
  4. Fix the with*() return values you were discarding.
  5. Re-read Security recommendations. Several defaults are stricter than the originals', and a few are still looser than a new deployment should accept.

docs.title: Names and attributes
docs.text:
A certificate names two parties — the subject and the issuer — and names them with a distinguished name, a structure from the directory specifications rather than from X.509. SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501 implements it, after X.501 and X.520.

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;

$name = Name::fromString('cn=example.com, o=ACME Ltd, c=FR');

echo $name->toString();                                       // cn=example.com,o=ACME Ltd,c=FR
echo $name->firstValueOf('cn')->stringValue();                // example.com

docs.title: The shape of a name
docs.text:
A Name is a sequence of RDNs — relative distinguished names — and each RDN is a set of AttributeTypeAndValue pairs. Three levels, because a name is a path through a directory and one step of that path may need more than one attribute to be unambiguous.

Name            cn=example.com, o=ACME Ltd, c=FR
└── RDN         c=FR
    └── ATV     type 2.5.4.6 (countryName), value "FR"

Almost every RDN holds exactly one attribute, so the nesting is invisible most of the time. It stops being invisible when you compare two names: see Comparing names.

The string form is written outermost-last

toString() follows RFC 2253: the RDNs come out in reverse order, so the most specific part is written first. cn=example.com,o=ACME Ltd,c=FR is a name whose first RDN — in the ASN.1 — is c=FR. all() gives the RDNs in ASN.1 order, not in string order.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Class Is ASN1\Name the whole name ASN1\RDN one step: a SET of attribute type and value pairs ASN1\AttributeTypeAndValue a type and its value ASN1\AttributeType the type, an OID with a known short name ASN1\AttributeValue\* the value, one class per standard type DN\DNParser the RFC 2253 string form, in and out MatchingRule\*, StringPrep\* the comparison rules

docs.title: Attributes elsewhere
docs.text:
The same Attribute machinery carries attributes that are not part of a name:

  • the extension request of a certification request;
  • the subjectDirectoryAttributes extension of a certificate;
  • the attributes an attribute certificate exists to carry.

See Attributes.

docs.title: Names in extensions
docs.text: A DN is not the only way a certificate names something. subjectAltName, issuerAltName, nameConstraints and the attribute certificate structures use GeneralName, which holds a DNS name, an email address, a URI, an IP address — or a DN, as one choice among several. See General names.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:

  • Attributes — the standard types, the value classes, collections.
  • General names — the nine choices and what each one holds.
  • Comparing names — why == is wrong and what equals() does instead.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: An attribute is a type and one or more values. The same structure appears in a distinguished name, in the extension request of a certification request, in the subjectDirectoryAttributes extension, and as the payload of an attribute certificate.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
AttributeType wraps an OID and knows the short names of the standard types:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeType;

$type = AttributeType::fromName('cn');
$type->oid();        // "2.5.4.3"
$type->typeName();   // "commonName"

$type = AttributeType::create('2.5.4.3');
AttributeType::attrNameToOID('emailAddress');   // "1.2.840.113549.1.9.1"

The table covers X.520 (2.5.4.*), the LDAP attributes of RFC 4519 and RFC 2798 — uid, mail, dc, memberOf — and the PKCS #9 emailAddress. Names are matched case-insensitively, and several types have aliases: mail is also rfc822Mailbox, dc is also domainComponent, email is also emailAddress and pkcs9email. An OID passed where a name is expected is returned as it is.

typeName() falls back to the OID for a type with no entry, so it is always safe to print.

docs.title: Values
The string type a value is written in
docs.text:
Most of these are DirectoryString values, which means their ASN.1 type is a choice: UTF8String, PrintableString, BMPString, UniversalString or TeletexString. create() writes a UTF8String unless you say otherwise:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\Feature\DirectoryString;

$value = CommonNameValue::create('example.com', DirectoryString::PRINTABLE);

Three types are not a directory string and are always written as a PrintableString: countryName, serialNumber and dnQualifier. Name::fromString() applies that rule for you — which is why a country code round-trips as a PrintableString and a common name as a UTF8String.

The string type is part of the encoding, not of the meaning

Two names that differ only in the string type of a value are still equal, because comparison transcodes before it compares. See Comparing names. The type still matters for an exact byte comparison, and for a peer that re-encodes what you sent.

docs.title: Values of an unknown type
docs.text:
An attribute whose OID has no class comes back as UnknownAttributeValue, which keeps the element as it was. Nothing is lost, and nothing throws:

$value->oid();           // the OID you were given
$value->stringValue();   // the element, as a string where that makes sense

If you later write a class for that type, Attribute::castValues() converts in place:

$attribute = $attribute->castValues(MyAttributeValue::class);

The class must derive from AttributeValue and declare the same OID.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Attribute holds a type and its values:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Attribute;

$attribute = Attribute::fromAttributeValues(CommonNameValue::create('example.com'));

$attribute->type();      // AttributeType
$attribute->oid();
$attribute->first();     // the first value
$attribute->values();    // all of them
count($attribute);

Two collections hold attributes, and they differ only in the ASN.1 they encode to:

Class, under ASN1\Collection Encodes to SequenceOfAttributes a SEQUENCE OF SetOfAttributes a SET OF

Both share the AttributeCollection API:

$attributes->has('cn');
$attributes->firstOf('cn');          // an Attribute
$attributes->allOf('cn');            // Attribute[]
$attributes->all();
$attributes = $attributes->withAdditional($attribute);
$attributes = $attributes->withUnique($attribute);   // replaces any attribute of the same type
count($attributes);

foreach ($attributes as $attribute) {
}

withUnique() is what you want for an attribute that must appear once: it replaces rather than appends.

docs.title: Writing a value class
docs.text:
Extend AttributeValue, or DirectoryString when the syntax is a directory string, and implement the four abstract methods plus fromASN1():

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\UTF8String;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\UnspecifiedType;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\AttributeValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\MatchingRule\CaseIgnoreMatch;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\MatchingRule\MatchingRule;

final class EmployeeNumberValue extends AttributeValue
{
    public const OID = '1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1';

    private function __construct(private readonly string $value)
    {
        parent::__construct(self::OID);
    }

    public static function create(string $value): self
    {
        return new self($value);
    }

    public static function fromASN1(UnspecifiedType $el): self
    {
        return self::create($el->asUTF8String()->string());
    }

    public function toASN1(): Element
    {
        return UTF8String::create($this->value);
    }

    public function stringValue(): string
    {
        return $this->value;
    }

    public function equalityMatchingRule(): MatchingRule
    {
        return CaseIgnoreMatch::create(Element::TYPE_UTF8_STRING);
    }

    public function rfc2253String(): string
    {
        return $this->value;
    }
}

equalityMatchingRule() is what name comparison uses, so choosing it is choosing how two of your values compare. Then toAttribute() and toAttributeTypeAndValue() come for free from the base class.

docs.title: Comparing names
docs.text:
Two certificates can name the same party with different bytes. One writes the common name as a PrintableString, the other as a BMPString; one writes ACME Ltd, the other acme ltd. Path validation has to chain an issuer DN to a subject DN across that, so comparison is a specified algorithm, not a string comparison.

$subject->equals($issuer);   // what you want
$subject->toString() === $issuer->toString();   // what you do not

docs.title: What equals() does
docs.text:
Three levels, following RFC 5280 section 7.1.

A Name is equal to another when they have the same number of RDNs and each RDN is equal to the one at its position.

An RDN is a SET, so two of them are equal when their attributes match as a multiset, in any order. Order is not part of the meaning.

An AttributeTypeAndValue is equal to another when the type OIDs match and the two values compare equal under their matching rules — each value prepared under its own syntax.

Each side is prepared under its own rule

Taking the matching rule from one side alone would push the other side's octets through the wrong transcoder, and then the same name written as a BMPString and as a PrintableString would compare as two different names. That is not a cosmetic bug: it means a directoryName a name constraint excludes becomes reachable by re-encoding it. Both sides are prepared under their own syntax, which is why equals() is the only comparison worth trusting.

docs.title: The matching rules
docs.text:
An attribute value chooses its rule in equalityMatchingRule().

Rule Compares CaseIgnoreMatch after string preparation, case-folded. The rule of every directory string CaseExactMatch after string preparation, case kept BinaryMatch octet by octet, no preparation

StringPrepMatchingRule is the base of the first two, and prepare() on it gives the prepared form of a value — useful when you want to index names, or to see why two values you expected to match do not:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\MatchingRule\CaseIgnoreMatch;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;

$rule = CaseIgnoreMatch::create(Element::TYPE_UTF8_STRING);

$rule->prepare('  ACME   Ltd  ');       // "acme ltd"
$rule->compare('ACME Ltd', 'acme  ltd'); // true

docs.title: String preparation
docs.text:
StringPreparer is the X.520 and RFC 4518 pipeline, in six steps:

Step Does STEP_TRANSCODE the string type's encoding to UTF-8 STEP_MAP case folding, and mapping the characters that map to nothing STEP_NORMALIZE Unicode normalisation STEP_PROHIBIT refuse the characters the specification forbids STEP_CHECK_BIDI refuse a string that mixes directions illegally STEP_INSIGNIFICANT_CHARS collapse the runs of space that carry no meaning 
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\StringPrep\StringPreparer;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Element;

$preparer = StringPreparer::forStringType(Element::TYPE_UTF8_STRING)->withCaseFolding(true);
$prepared = $preparer->prepare($value);

A string the prohibit or bidi step refuses raises StringPreparationException. Preparation is where mbstring is required: this is the step that needs it.

docs.title: The cost of comparing
docs.text:
A multi-valued RDN makes the multiset question real, and pairing the two sides off one at a time costs a comparison for every pair — work quadratic in the number of attributes, each step preparing a string afresh. An RDN whose attributes an attacker put in the reverse order would make you pay for it.

So where the matching rules can name their values, the attributes are grouped by that name and the answer takes one pass. AttributeTypeAndValue::comparisonKey() is that name: the type OID, the rule class and the prepared value, or null for a rule that cannot produce one. Two attributes are equal exactly when their keys are identical.

You can use it yourself to index names — as a hash map key, or a database column — rather than comparing every pair:

$key = $attributeTypeAndValue->comparisonKey();   // string, or null

docs.title: Comparing certificates, not names
docs.text:
The questions above are about names. For certificates:

$a->equals($b);                     // the two encodings, octet by octet
$a->hasEqualSubjectIdentity($b);    // same subject, same key, same serial number

hasEqualSubjectIdentity() is not an identity check

Two certificates can agree on subject, key and serial number and still be issued by different issuers with different extensions. It answers a narrow question; do not use it to decide that two certificates are interchangeable.

CertificateBundle::contains() is built on equals(), so a trust store lookup is an exact-encoding lookup. See Bundles and chains.

docs.title: From a string
docs.text:
The quickest way in, and what you will use most:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;

$name = Name::fromString('cn=example.com, o=ACME Ltd, c=FR');

The short names come from the LDAP attribute registry and are matched case-insensitively, so CN, cn and commonName are the same type. An OID works too, for a type with no short name:

$name = Name::fromString('2.5.4.3=example.com');

A name the parser does not recognise raises OutOfBoundsException with the name in the message.

docs.title: Escaping
docs.text:
RFC 2253 reserves , = + < > # ;, and a value holding one has to escape it. DNParser does it for you:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\DN\DNParser;

$value = DNParser::escapeString('ACME Ltd, Paris');     // ACME Ltd\, Paris
$name = Name::fromString('o=' . $value . ',c=FR');

Never build a DN by concatenating values you did not escape

An unescaped comma in a value does not fail: it ends the RDN and starts another one, so o=ACME Ltd, Paris parses as two attributes and the name you get is not the name you meant. Escape every value you interpolate, or build the name from objects.

A value may also be written as a hex string — cn=#0C0B6578616D706C652E636F6D — which the parser reads as a DER element and keeps as it was. That is how a value whose string type matters survives a round trip.

docs.title: From objects
docs.text:
Building a name from objects skips the string form, and its escaping, entirely:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\CommonNameValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\CountryNameValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\OrganizationNameValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\RDN;

$name = Name::create(
    RDN::fromAttributeValues(CountryNameValue::create('FR')),
    RDN::fromAttributeValues(OrganizationNameValue::create('ACME Ltd, Paris')),
    RDN::fromAttributeValues(CommonNameValue::create('example.com'))
);

echo $name->toString();   // cn=example.com,o=ACME Ltd\, Paris,c=FR

Note the order: Name::create() takes the RDNs in ASN.1 order, outermost first, which is the reverse of how the string form reads them.

docs.title: Reading one
docs.text:
$name = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->subject();

echo $name->toString();                         // the RFC 2253 string
count($name);                                   // how many RDNs
$name->all();                                   // RDN[], in ASN.1 order

$name->firstValueOf('cn')->stringValue();       // the first common name
$name->countOfType('cn');                       // how many there are

firstValueOf() throws RangeException when the type is absent, and when one RDN carries it more than once — an ambiguous question gets an error rather than an arbitrary answer. Ask first:

if ($name->countOfType('cn') === 1) {
    $cn = $name->firstValueOf('cn')->stringValue();
}

Walking the structure yourself:

foreach ($name as $rdn) {
    foreach ($rdn as $attributeTypeAndValue) {
        $attributeTypeAndValue->oid();                      // "2.5.4.3"
        $attributeTypeAndValue->type()->typeName();         // "commonName"
        $attributeTypeAndValue->value()->stringValue();     // "example.com"
    }
}

docs.title: Multi-valued RDNs
docs.text:
One RDN may hold several attributes, which means one step of the name needs all of them to be unambiguous:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\CommonNameValue;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\AttributeValue\OrganizationalUnitNameValue;

$rdn = RDN::fromAttributeValues(
    CommonNameValue::create('J. Smith'),
    OrganizationalUnitNameValue::create('Sales')
);

echo $rdn->toString();   // cn=J. Smith+ou=Sales

The + is how RFC 2253 joins them, and Name::fromString() reads it back. $rdn->allOf('cn') returns every value of one type within the RDN.

Rare in practice, and worth knowing about for one reason: it is where name comparison stops being a string comparison. See Comparing names.

docs.title: The empty name
docs.text: Name::create() with no arguments is a valid, empty name. RFC 5280 allows it for a subject, provided the certificate carries a subjectAltName marked critical. TBSCertificate::fromCSR() starts from one for the issuer, which withIssuerCertificate() then fills in.

docs.title: To and from ASN.1
docs.text:
$sequence = $name->toASN1();
$name = Name::fromASN1($sequence);

$der = $name->toASN1()->toDER();

Name has no fromDER(): decode the Sequence first.

docs.title: General names
docs.text:
A distinguished name is not the only way a certificate names something. subjectAltName, issuerAltName, nameConstraints, the CRL distribution points and the attribute certificate structures all use GeneralName, a choice of nine.

For a TLS certificate, this is where the hostname actually lives: the common name is a convention the web PKI abandoned, and subjectAltName is normative.

docs.title: The nine choices
docs.text: Tag Class, under X509\GeneralName Holds TAG_OTHER_NAME OtherName an OID and any element TAG_RFC822_NAME RFC822Name an email address TAG_DNS_NAME DNSName a host name TAG_X400_ADDRESS X400Address an X.400 address, kept as a Sequence TAG_DIRECTORY_NAME DirectoryName a Name TAG_EDI_PARTY_NAME EDIPartyName an EDI party name, kept as a Sequence TAG_URI UniformResourceIdentifier a URI TAG_IP_ADDRESS IPv4Address, IPv6Address an address, and in a name constraint a mask TAG_REGISTERED_ID RegisteredID an OID

docs.title: Building them
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X501\ASN1\Name;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DirectoryName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralNames;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\IPv4Address;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\RFC822Name;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\UniformResourceIdentifier;

$names = GeneralNames::create(
    DNSName::create('example.com'),
    DNSName::create('www.example.com'),
    RFC822Name::create('admin@example.com'),
    UniformResourceIdentifier::create('https://example.com/'),
    IPv4Address::create('192.0.2.1'),
    DirectoryName::create(Name::fromString('cn=example.com'))
);

X400Address and EDIPartyName take a Sequence: the library carries them without modelling their contents, which nothing in a modern PKI uses.

OtherName is the escape hatch — an OID and any element:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\ASN1\Type\Primitive\UTF8String;
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\OtherName;

$name = OtherName::create('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1', UTF8String::create('whatever your schema says'));

docs.title: Reading them
docs.text:
GeneralNames is a collection, with shortcuts for the three types you usually want:

$names = $certificate->tbsCertificate()->extensions()->subjectAlternativeName()->names();

$names->firstDNS();   // the first DNS name, as a string
$names->firstURI();   // the first URI
$names->firstDN();    // the first directory name, as a Name

Each throws when there is none of that type. Ask first, or walk the collection:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\GeneralName;

if ($names->has(GeneralName::TAG_DNS_NAME)) {
    foreach ($names->allOf(GeneralName::TAG_DNS_NAME) as $name) {
        /** @var \SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\DNSName $name */
        echo $name->name();
    }
}

$names->firstOf(GeneralName::TAG_IP_ADDRESS);
count($names);

Every GeneralName answers string() and (string), so printing one needs no type switch. For the value in its own shape, the accessor differs by class:

$dnsName->name();
$rfc822Name->email();
$uri->uri();
$directoryName->dn();              // a Name
$registeredID->oid();
$ipAddress->address();
$ipAddress->mask();                // only in a name constraint
$otherName->type();                // the OID

docs.title: Comparing them
docs.text:
$a->equals($b);

Two general names are equal when they are the same choice and their encodings agree, octet for octet.

GeneralName::equals() is a byte comparison, including for a directory name

It compares the DER of the two choices, so a DirectoryName whose Name says the same thing in a different string type is not equal under it. For the semantic question, take the names out and use Name::equals():

$a->dn()->equals($b->dn());   // the X.501 rules, see Comparing names

Name constraint processing inside path validation already does the right thing: it compares a directoryName constraint against a subject with the name comparison rules, not with this method.

docs.title: Addresses and masks
docs.text:
IPv4Address and IPv6Address take an optional mask, and the mask is only meaningful in a name constraint, where the pair describes a subnet:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\GeneralName\IPv4Address;

IPv4Address::create('192.0.2.1');                     // in a subjectAltName
IPv4Address::create('192.0.2.0', '255.255.255.0');    // in a nameConstraints

Calling mask() on an address that has none throws LogicException.

A hostname in a certificate is not a hostname you matched

firstDNS() gives you the string the issuer wrote. Deciding whether it names the server you meant to reach — wildcards, trailing dots, internationalised domains, the rules of the protocol you are speaking — is a step of your own that this library does not perform, and that path validation never looks at.

docs.title: Textual encoding (PEM)
docs.text:
DER is bytes. PEM is those bytes in base64 between two labelled lines, which is how certificates and keys travel through files, configuration and copy-paste. SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding reads and writes it, after RFC 7468.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIDdzCCAl+gAwIBAgIEAgAAuTANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQUFADBaMQswCQYDVQQGEwJJ
…
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

docs.title: One block
docs.text:
use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEM;

$pem = PEM::fromFile('/etc/ssl/certs/server.crt');
$pem = PEM::fromString($text);
$pem = PEM::create(PEM::TYPE_CERTIFICATE, $der);

$pem->type();     // "CERTIFICATE", the label between the dashes
$pem->data();     // the DER bytes
$pem->string();   // the whole block, with its dashes and line breaks
echo $pem;        // the same

fromString() reads the first block of the string and ignores what surrounds it, so a certificate pasted into a mail body still parses.

docs.title: The labels
docs.text:
Constant Label TYPE_CERTIFICATE CERTIFICATE TYPE_CRL X509 CRL TYPE_CERTIFICATE_REQUEST CERTIFICATE REQUEST TYPE_ATTRIBUTE_CERTIFICATE ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE TYPE_PRIVATE_KEY PRIVATE KEY TYPE_ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY TYPE_PUBLIC_KEY PUBLIC KEY TYPE_RSA_PRIVATE_KEY RSA PRIVATE KEY TYPE_RSA_PUBLIC_KEY RSA PUBLIC KEY TYPE_EC_PRIVATE_KEY EC PRIVATE KEY TYPE_PKCS7 PKCS7 TYPE_CMS CMS

A label the list does not name is still read: type() gives it back as it was written.

The label says what the bytes are meant to be, and nothing checks that it is true. Certificate::fromPEM() and the other fromPEM() methods assert the label they need and refuse a block that carries another one, so a private key handed to a certificate parser fails there rather than decoding into something unexpected.

docs.title: A bundle
docs.text:
A file holding several blocks — a chain, a trust store — is a PEMBundle:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\CryptoEncoding\PEMBundle;

$bundle = PEMBundle::fromFile('/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt');

count($bundle);        // how many blocks
$bundle->first();      // the first PEM
$bundle->last();       // the last
$bundle->all();        // PEM[]

foreach ($bundle as $pem) {
    // in the order the file has them
}

echo $bundle->string();   // every block, back to back

Each block is read on its own, so a bundle may mix labels: a key and its certificate in one file comes back as two PEM objects with different types.

Turning a bundle into certificates is one call:

use SpomkyLabs\Pki\X509\Certificate\CertificateBundle;

$certificates = CertificateBundle::fromPEMBundle($bundle);

See Bundles and chains.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
file_put_contents('server.crt', $certificate->toPEM()->string());

toPEM() exists on Certificate, CertificationRequest, AttributeCertificate, PublicKeyInfo, OneAsymmetricKey and the key classes, each with the right label.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
PEM::fromString() and PEMBundle::fromString() throw UnexpectedValueException when there is no block to read, or when the base64 is not valid.

RFC 7468 section 3 asks for the padded base64 alphabet of RFC 4648. PHP's base64_decode() is strict about the alphabet but not about the padding, so a payload whose length is not a multiple of four — one OpenSSL would refuse — is refused here too rather than decoded into fewer bytes than it looks like.

Encrypted private keys are not decrypted

PEM reads a block labelled ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY and hands you its bytes, but those bytes are ciphertext and there is no class that models them: the library has no password-based key derivation, and OneAsymmetricKey::fromPEM() refuses that label. Decrypt it elsewhere — openssl pkey -in key.pem -out plain.pem, for one — and read the result.

A PEM bundle from a peer holds as many blocks as they chose to send. Count them before you walk them; see Decoding untrusted input.
